pages.title: Configuration
pages.description: One typed config module validated with Zod 4 at boot and frozen, read from the environment, failing fast on a missing secret.
headings: Do not branch on NODEENV deep in the code
pages.text: Configuration is everything that differs between your laptop, staging and production. Get it wrong and you find out at 3am, because a missing environment variable becomes undefined, and undefined becomes a connection string of "undefined" twenty minutes into a deploy. The fix is to read the environment once, validate it against a schema at startup, and refuse to boot if anything is missing. Why it exists Three failure modes justify the whole pattern. Silent undefined. process.env.STRIPESECRET for a variable that was never set is undefined, not an error. The process starts, serves health checks, passes the readiness probe, and fails on the first payment. Nothing in JavaScript stops you. Type confusion. Everything in process.env is a string. process.env.PORT is "3000", process.env.ENABLECACHE is "false" — and "false" is truthy. Number(process.env.MAXPOOL) for an unset variable is NaN, which propagates silently into a pool size. Scattered reads. When process.env is read in forty files, nobody can answer "what does this service need to run?" without grepping, and no test can override a value without mutating global state. One module, validated once, solves all three. The twelve-factor rule Store config in the environment. Config lives in environment variables, not in files that get committed, and not in config/production.json selected by NODEENV. The reasons are practical: The same build artifact — the same container image, the same git SHA — runs in every environment. If configuration is baked into the image, staging and production are different builds and you are not testing what you ship. Environment variables are language-agnostic and every platform can inject them. Secrets never touch the repository. A committed config/production.json is a leaked credential with extra steps. What belongs in the environment: anything that varies by deployment, and anything secret. What does not: application constants like a page size default or a retry count — those are code, and putting them in the environment gives you an operational lever nobody will ever pull correctly. Basic example One module. It reads process.env, validates it, exits on failure, and exports a frozen object. Everything else imports config, never process.env: Best practice Make process.env illegal outside src/config.js with a lint rule — ESLint's no-restricted-properties or no-process-env. It is the onl

pages.title: Graceful shutdown
pages.description: The exact ordering that lets a Node process stop without dropping requests, and the load-balancer and keep-alive races that cause 502s even when your code is correct.
headings: The sequence, and why the order matters
The 502 race nobody tells you about
keepAliveTimeout must exceed the proxy's idle timeout
pages.text: Every deploy kills your process. A rolling update on Kubernetes, an ECS task replacement, a systemctl restart, an autoscaler scaling in — all of them send SIGTERM and then wait a fixed number of seconds before sending SIGKILL. What happens in those seconds decides whether your users see 502s on every deploy or nothing at all. This page is about the operational sequencing: what order the steps go in, why each one is where it is, and the two races that produce dropped requests even when the shutdown code is perfect. Process management covers the surrounding topic — supervisors, restart policies, and the process lifecycle. Why it exists By default, process.on('SIGTERM') has no handler and Node exits immediately. Immediately means: Every in-flight request dies mid-response. The client sees a connection reset, not a status code. Database transactions that were open are rolled back by the server, eventually, after a timeout. A job pulled off a queue but not yet acknowledged is either lost or redelivered, depending on the broker. Connections in your pool are closed by the OS rather than by a protocol-level goodbye, so the database logs a burst of unexpected disconnects. Multiply that by the number of pods times the number of deploys per day. A team deploying ten times a day with fifty pods drops a few thousand requests a week for want of about sixty lines of code. The sequence, and why the order matters There are seven steps and the order is not negotiable. Each one exists to close a window the previous one opened. # Step Why it must be here 1 Flip readiness to false Load balancers stop sending new connections. This has to be first, and it has to happen well before the socket closes, because deregistration is not instant. 2 server.close() Stop accepting new connections and stop reusing idle keep-alive ones. Existing in-flight requests keep running. 3 server.closeIdleConnections() Keep-alive sockets with no active request survive server.close() forever. This closes them so the callback can actually fire. 4 Wait for in-flight requests, with a hard deadline The whole point. The deadline exists because one stuck handler must not hold the process past SIGKILL. 5 Drain queues and workers A job handler is an in-flight request that HTTP does not know about. Stop consuming, finish or return what is held. 6 Close DB pools and Redis After step 4 and 5, never before — closing

pages.title: Clustering
pages.description: Using node:cluster to spread work across CPU cores, when it actually helps, and why one process per container is usually right in Kubernetes.
headings: In Kubernetes, run one process per container
workerthreads is usually the better answer for CPU work
pages.text: A Node process runs your JavaScript on one thread. On a machine with sixteen cores that means fifteen of them sit idle unless you do something about it. node:cluster is the built-in answer: fork one process per core and let the operating system share a listening socket between them. Whether you should is a different question, and the honest answer for most containerised deployments is no. How it works cluster.fork() spawns a child process running the same script. The primary creates the listening socket; workers inherit it. On Linux, Node uses SOREUSEPORT-style round-robin distribution by default, so the primary hands accepted connections to workers rather than letting the kernel decide — which avoids the pathological imbalance the kernel's own accept queue produces. Workers are separate operating-system processes. They share no memory, no variables, no module state. Each one has its own V8 heap, its own JIT-compiled code, its own connection pool. Communication is message passing over an IPC channel, which is JSON serialization — never a substitute for shared state. Basic example availableParallelism() is the right function to call. It is not os.cpus().length. Warning os.cpus().length reports the host's core count, not what your container is allowed to use. A container with --cpus=1 on a 64-core node still sees 64 entries in os.cpus(), so os.cpus().length forks 64 workers that fight over a single core's worth of CPU quota. Throughput drops, latency rises, and memory goes up 64-fold. availableParallelism() (Node 18.14+) respects CPU affinity and cgroup limits where the platform exposes them. Use it, and still allow an explicit WEBCONCURRENCY override, because no API detects every platform's quota correctly. When clustering helps A CPU-bound workload on a multi-core machine you control. Template rendering, image processing, JSON serialization of large payloads, cryptography that is not on a threadpool, data transformation. If a CPU profile shows your JavaScript actually executing rather than waiting, more processes means more throughput, close to linearly, up to the core count. A single VM or bare-metal host running one service. You paid for sixteen cores; one process uses one. Here clustering is the whole point, and a supervisor like PM2 exists to do it for you. Fault isolation on a long-running process. A worker that hits an uncaught exception dies and is re

pages.title: Health and readiness probes
pages.description: Liveness, readiness and startup probes — what each one should actually check, the failure mode of getting each wrong, and how readiness ties into graceful shutdown.
pages.text: Three probes, three different questions, three different answers. Conflating them is one of the few configuration mistakes that can take down a healthy fleet: a liveness probe that checks the database will restart every pod you have the moment the database has a bad ten seconds. The three questions Probe Question Failure action Should it check dependencies? Liveness Is this process broken beyond recovery? Restart the container No. Never. Readiness Should this instance receive traffic right now? Remove from the load balancer; keep it running Yes — the ones it cannot serve without Startup Has it finished booting yet? Keep waiting, then restart if it never starts Boot progress only The distinction is entirely about what the platform does when the probe fails. Liveness failure destroys the container. Readiness failure removes traffic and leaves it alive to recover. That difference dictates what each may legitimately check. Liveness: is the process wedged? A liveness probe answers one question: would restarting this container fix it? The only conditions that qualify are ones the process cannot recover from on its own — a deadlocked event loop, an unrecoverable internal state, a heap that is exhausted and thrashing GC. So a liveness endpoint does almost nothing: That looks too simple to be useful. It is not. Reaching this handler means the event loop is turning, the HTTP server is accepting connections, and the router is intact. If the event loop were blocked, the probe would time out — which is exactly the condition a restart fixes. Danger Never check a database, a cache, or any other service from a liveness probe. This is the single most damaging health-check mistake, and it turns a partial outage into a total one. The failure: your database has a five-second blip — a failover, a lock storm, a network partition. Every pod's liveness probe fails at the same instant. Kubernetes kills every pod in your Deployment simultaneously. They restart, immediately re-check the still-recovering database, fail again, and enter CrashLoopBackOff. Now the database recovers — and there is nothing left to serve traffic. Restarts back off exponentially, so recovery takes minutes longer than the original blip. You have converted a five-second database hiccup into a multi-minute total outage, and every restart added reconnection load to the database that was already struggling. Restar

pages.title: Observability
pages.description: Structured logs with pino, correlation IDs via AsyncLocalStorage, the metrics that actually matter, OpenTelemetry tracing, and alerting on symptoms rather than causes.
pages.text: Monitoring tells you that something is wrong. Observability lets you work out why without shipping new code. The difference matters at 3am, when the dashboard says error rate is up and the only question is which of forty things caused it. The three signals Signal Answers Cardinality Cost model Typical retention Logs What happened to this request? Unbounded — any field, any value Per byte ingested Days to weeks Metrics How is the system behaving overall? Must be bounded — every label combination is a time series Per series, per interval Months to years Traces Where did the time go, across services? High, usually sampled Per span Days They are not substitutes. Metrics show that p99 latency doubled; a trace shows which downstream call caused it; a log line shows the exact query and the user it affected. Skipping one means the other two do more work than they should — most commonly, teams with no metrics try to derive rates from logs, which is both expensive and slow. Add them in that order: structured logs first, then RED metrics, then tracing when you have more than one service. Structured logging with pino Log objects, not sentences. console.log('user ' + id + ' failed login') is unsearchable — you cannot filter, count, or aggregate on it. A JSON line with typed fields can be queried like a table. pino 10.3.1 is the right default. It serializes to JSON on the fly with very little overhead, which matters because logging sits on the request path. Rules that hold regardless of library: Write JSON to stdout and stop there. The platform collects stdout. An application that writes to a file, rotates it, or ships it itself is doing work the platform already does, and it will get it wrong. pino-pretty 13.1.3 is a development dependency. Pipe to it locally (node src/server.js | pino-pretty); never run it in production, where it costs CPU to produce a format nothing parses. Log levels mean something. error is "a human should look at this". warn is "unusual but handled". info is business events — a user registered, an order was placed. debug is off in production. If error fires a thousand times an hour, it is not an error and people will stop reading it. Log a message once, at the boundary. Logging the same failure in the repository, the service and the error handler produces three lines that look like three problems. Never log secrets or PII. Redaction is a safety net,

pages.title: Dockerfile
pages.description: A multi-stage Dockerfile for Node 24 — pinned base image, npm ci, layer caching, non-root user, correct PID 1 signal handling, and no secrets in any layer.
pages.text: A Node Dockerfile is about six instructions long and almost everyone gets at least two of them wrong. The consequences are not cosmetic: the wrong CMD means SIGTERM never reaches your process and every deploy drops requests; a secret in a build arg is permanently readable in the image; running as root turns a container escape into a host compromise. The complete Dockerfile If you have no build step, delete stage 2 and copy src/ in stage 3 instead of dist/. The .dockerignore Write this before the Dockerfile. Without it, COPY . . sends your entire working directory to the daemon — including nodemodules built for your laptop's architecture, your .git history, and your .env. Danger A missing .dockerignore is how a .env ends up inside a published image. COPY . . copies it, the layer is immutable, and docker history plus a filesystem extract retrieves it — deleting the file in a later RUN does not remove it from the earlier layer. If a secret has ever been in a layer, it is compromised. Rotate it; do not rebuild and hope. Pin the base image FROM node:latest means your build is not reproducible and today's rebuild may run a different major of Node than yesterday's. FROM node:24 is better but still floats across patch releases. Pin Reproducible Gets security patches Use for node:latest No Yes, and major upgrades you did not ask for Never node:24 No Yes, on rebuild Local experiments node:24-bookworm-slim No Yes, on rebuild Reasonable default node:24.20.0-bookworm-slim Mostly Only when you bump it Production node:24-bookworm-slim@sha256:… Exactly Only when you bump it Production with a bot that bumps it Digest pinning is the strongest guarantee: the same digest is byte-identical forever. Its cost is that you stop receiving base-image security patches until something updates the digest, so pair it with Dependabot or Renovate. Substitute the real digest from docker pull output — do not copy a placeholder. pages.text: CI exists to catch, before merge, the things that are expensive to catch after. For a Node service that means four questions: does it install from the lockfile, does it lint, do the tests pass against a real database, and does the artifact you are about to ship actually boot. The workflow Note actions/checkout@v7 (v7.0.1) and actions/setup-node@v7 (v7.0.0) were the current majors on 2026-09-09. Newer majors are released regularly — check each action's repository rather than assuming these are still latest. Pin the major at minimum; pin the full commit SHA if your threat model includes a compromised action. Checkout and setup-node actions/setup-node does two jobs, and the second is the one people skip. node-version-file: .nvmrc instead of a hardcoded node-version: 24. One file is then the source of truth for your laptop, your version manager and CI. A team that hardcodes the version in the workflow eventually tests on a version nobody develops against. See Prerequisites. cache: npm caches the npm download cache — not nodemodules — keyed on package-lock.json. Restore is fast and correctness is preserved, because npm ci still resolves from the lockfile rather than reusing an installed tree. Caching nodemodules directly is the version of this that goes wrong: a stale tree survives a lockfile change and CI tests something that does not exist. Set cache-dependency-path if your lockfile is not at the repository root. npm ci, never npm install npm ci deletes nodemodules, installs exactly what package-lock.json specifies, and fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree. npm install resolves ranges and quietly rewrites the lockfile. In CI that difference is the whole point. With npm install, a job can pass against a dependency tree that exists nowhere else — not in your repository, not on anyone's machine, not in the image you deploy. The lockfile-mismatch failure is a feature too: it catches the pull request where someone edited package.json by hand. Lint ESLint 10.10.0 uses flat config (eslint.config.js). Run it on the whole tree, not on changed files — a rule change affects everything, and partial linting hides that. Keep lint in the same job as the tests unless it is slow. A separate job costs another checkout and another install for a step that usually takes seconds. Add --max-warnings=0 if you want warnings to be blocking. Warnings that never block accumulat

pages.title: Performance
pages.description: Measuring before optimizing, the event loop as the real bottleneck, and why the database usually dominates everything else you might tune.
headings: The event loop is the bottleneck
Never call a synchronous API on the request path
Outbound calls: keep-alive and agent reuse
pages.text: Almost every Node performance discussion is about the wrong thing. Teams tune JSON serialization while a missing index costs them 400 ms per request. The discipline is simple and rarely followed: measure, find the largest cost, fix that, measure again. Measure first You cannot reason your way to a bottleneck. Intuition about JavaScript performance is wrong often enough that acting on it is a coin flip, and the cost of guessing wrong is a week of work that changes nothing. Three tools, three different questions. Load generation autocannon — a Node HTTP benchmarking tool, the fastest way to get a latency distribution for one endpoint. -c connections, -d duration in seconds, -p pipelined requests per connection. It reports requests per second and a latency table including p97.5 and p99. k6 — a scriptable load tester for realistic scenarios: a login, then a search, then a purchase, with think time and ramping virtual users. Use it when the shape of the traffic matters, which it does as soon as you have more than one endpoint. Warning A benchmark against an empty database on your laptop measures nothing useful. Production has a table with ten million rows, a network hop to the database, TLS, cold caches, and a connection pool shared with forty other replicas. Load-test against a realistic dataset in a realistic environment, or you will optimize for a system you do not run. Benchmark from a different machine than the one running the server, too. Otherwise the load generator competes with the application for the CPU you are trying to measure. CPU profiling --cpu-prof is built in. Run the process under load, stop it, and open the resulting .cpuprofile in Chrome DevTools or VS Code. Read it bottom-up: the functions with the most self time are where the CPU actually went. A wide, flat profile with everything in libuv and V8 internals means you are I/O-bound and there is no CPU problem to solve. For a running production process you can attach the inspector instead — node --inspect plus a profiler session — but never expose the inspector port; see Debugging. Heap snapshots (--heap-prof, or writeHeapSnapshot()) answer a different question: what is retaining memory. Take two under steady load, several minutes apart, and compare. Objects whose count only ever grows are your leak. Diagnosis clinic wraps the above with automatic interpretation. clinic doctor runs your app un

pages.text: Work through this before the first production deploy, and again before any release that changes how the service is exposed, authenticated or stored. Every item is one line and links to the page that explains why it is here — the checklist is an index, not a substitute for the reasoning. Not every item applies to every service. Deciding an item does not apply is fine; skipping it because you did not read it is not. Configuration and secrets [ ] All configuration comes from environment variables, not committed files — Configuration [ ] A single config.js is validated with Zod 4 at boot and exported frozen — Configuration [ ] The process exits non-zero when a required variable is missing, before binding a port — Configuration [ ] No secret has a fallback default anywhere in the codebase — Configuration [ ] process.env is read in exactly one module, enforced by a lint rule — Configuration [ ] No NODEENV branch exists in business logic — Configuration [ ] NODEENV=production is set in the image; staging uses it too, with a separate APPENV label — Dockerfile [ ] .env is in .gitignore and .dockerignore; only .env.example is committed — Running the examples [ ] Secrets are injected from a secret store, not baked into the image or a build arg — Secrets management [ ] No secret appears in docker history, docker inspect, or any image layer — Dockerfile [ ] Every environment has its own credentials; staging cannot reach production data — Secrets management [ ] Secret rotation has been performed once, as a drill, without downtime — Secrets management [ ] The safe (non-secret) config view is logged once at boot with the git SHA — Observability [ ] Feature flags default to off and each has a removal date — Configuration HTTP security headers [ ] helmet 8.3.0 is registered before the routes — Security headers with Helmet [ ] A Content-Security-Policy is set and tested, not left at the default for an API that serves HTML — Security headers [ ] HSTS is enabled with a meaningful max-age, after confirming HTTPS works everywhere — HTTPS and TLS [ ] X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and a frame-ancestors policy are present — Security headers [ ] x-powered-by is disabled — Security headers with Helmet [ ] CORS uses an explicit origin allow-list; no reflected origin, no with credentials — CORS misconfiguration [ ] app.set('trust proxy', …) matches your actual proxy depth — Request and

This page is the only place on the site where Express 4 APIs appear — everywhere else the build fails on them. Work through it top to bottom when you upgrade: removals first (they throw or 404), then changed behavior (it silently does something different), then the procedure and the done-checklist at the end. pages.text: Find the error text, read the cause, apply the fix. Every entry links to the page that explains the underlying mechanism properly — this page is a lookup table, not a substitute for understanding. Modules and startup Error [ERRREQUIREESM]: require() of ES Module … not supported Cause. A CommonJS file is require()-ing an ESM-only package. Node 24 can require() an ES module, but only one with no top-level await anywhere in its graph — so this now appears mainly for packages that use top-level await, or on older runtimes. file-type and nanoid are the two you will meet most often. Fix. Move your project to ESM, which is where everything is heading anyway: Then convert require() to import. If one file must stay CommonJS, use a dynamic import, which always works: More: ESM vs CommonJS. SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module Cause. The opposite direction: a .js file containing import is being parsed as CommonJS, because the nearest package.json has no "type": "module". Fix. Add "type": "module" to package.json, or rename the file to .mjs. Do not "fix" it by rewriting import to require — that trades a one-line fix for a permanent constraint. More: ESM vs CommonJS. ReferenceError: dirname is not defined in ES module scope Cause. dirname, filename, require and module are CommonJS wrapper variables. ES modules do not have them. Fix. On Node 24 use import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename: The portable form, if you need to support an older runtime: More: Files and paths. Routing TypeError: Missing parameter name at 1: https://git.new/pathToRegexpError Cause. An Express 4 route pattern reached path-to-regexp@8. A or : with nothing usable after it — almost always the old catch-all '/', or a stray : in a literal path. The number is the character offset in the path string. This throws while the route is being registered, so the process dies at boot and no error middleware can catch it. Fix. Name the wildcard, and wrap it in a group if it must also match the mount root: Old New '/' '/{splat}' (matches / too) or '/splat' (does not) '/files/' '/files/path' — req.params.path is an array More: Route parameters and path syntax, Express 4 → 5 migration. TypeError: Unexpected ? at 7, expected END: https://git.new/pathToRegexpError Cause. (, ), [, ], ?, + and ! are reserved in path-to-regexp v8. The ? suffix modifier, inline regex groups and the '/[a|b]/:slug'

pages.title: Introduction and when to choose Nest
pages.description: What NestJS 12 actually is, the module and dependency-injection model it imposes, and an honest account of when it beats plain Express and when it does not.
headings: Why the DI container is the point
When to choose Nest over plain Express
pages.text: NestJS is an application framework that sits on top of an HTTP platform — Express 5 by default — and replaces "wire it up however you like" with a fixed architecture: modules that declare what they own, providers resolved by a dependency-injection container, and a request pipeline with named stages. Version 12 is the current line: @nestjs/core and @nestjs/common are 12.0.1, they ship as ES modules, and @nestjs/platform-express@12.0.1 bundles express@5.2.1. What Nest actually is Three things, and it is worth separating them because you can adopt one without loving the others. Layer What it gives you What it costs A DI container Constructor injection, one instance per module graph, swap any dependency in a test Decorators, reflect-metadata, a real build step A module system An explicit graph of what each feature imports, provides and exports Boilerplate for small apps; a second mental model on top of ES modules A request pipeline Middleware, guards, interceptors, pipes and exception filters as first-class, composable stages Indirection — the path from URL to handler is not a single file you can read top to bottom Underneath all of it is still Express. Nest builds an Express app, registers your controllers as routes on it, and hands requests to your handlers. That is why every Express 5 rule from Part 1 still applies here — see How Nest uses Express. The architecture in one example A feature is a module. The module owns a controller (HTTP in, HTTP out) and a service (the rules). The controller does not construct the service; it declares that it needs one. Three files say what four hundred lines of manual wiring would: this controller needs that service, this module publishes that service to whoever imports it, and nothing else can reach it. The container does the construction, so a test can construct the controller with a fake service and never open a socket. Note The constructor above assigns the field explicitly rather than using the constructor(private readonly users: UsersService) shorthand. Both are identical to Nest. The reason for the longer form is explained in Dependency injection — it is a TypeScript erasability question, not a Nest one. Why the DI container is the point Every other feature is downstream of it. Guards, interceptors and pipes can be classes with injected dependencies because there is a container to resolve them. @nestjs/config, @nestjs

headings: What a new project depends on
pages.text: @nestjs/cli is 12.0.0 and it is the only supported way to scaffold, build and run a Nest project. It wraps TypeScript compilation, watch mode, the schematics that generate files, and — new in v12 — a deploy command. The one thing that surprises people is that the CLI needs a newer Node than the app it builds. The Node version floor Two different floors apply, and they are not the same number. To do this Needs Node Why Run a Nest 12 app v20.19+, v22.12+, or v26+ @nestjs/core@12.0.1 declares engines.node: ">= 20", and the ESM packages need a runtime with require(esm) Use the CLI — nest new, nest generate, nest build, nest upgrade v22.22.3+, v24.15+, or v26+ @nestjs/schematics@12.0.0 declares engines.node: ">=22.12.0" because of the Angular devkit underneath This handbook targets Node 24 LTS (24.20.0 at the time of writing), which satisfies both with room to spare. Node 20 is end of life as of 2026-04-30 — do not start there even though @nestjs/core still accepts it. Warning A CI image pinned to Node 20 or 22.12 will install @nestjs/cli and then fail inside a schematic with an engine error that names @angular-devkit/schematics, not Nest. If nest new or nest generate dies with a message about an unsupported engine, check node -v before anything else. Installing Install the CLI globally, or do not install it at all and let npx fetch it per invocation. The npx form is what belongs in a CI script and in a README, because it makes the CLI version part of the repository rather than part of whoever's laptop ran the command. nest new nest new asks for a package manager if you do not pass --package-manager, creates the directory, writes the project files, and installs dependencies. Useful flags: Flag Effect --package-manager <npm|pnpm|yarn> skips the interactive prompt --skip-install writes files, installs nothing — what you want in a template repository --skip-git no git init --directory <path> generate into a directory whose name differs from the project name --dry-run print what would be written and exit --strict turn on TypeScript's strict family in the generated tsconfig.json Use --strict. The generated project without it has strictNullChecks off, and turning strict mode on later in a codebase that grew without it is a week of work. pages.title: Project structure
pages.description: What nest new generates, how to grow it into a feature-first layout, and which layering rules from plain Express still apply inside a Nest codebase.
pages.text: nest new gives you a working four-file application and no opinion about what happens next. The default layout is fine for a tutorial and wrong for anything with more than one feature, so the useful question is not "what did the CLI generate" but "what does this tree look like at forty endpoints". What the CLI generates main.ts is the only file that knows a server exists. Everything else describes a graph of modules, and NestFactory.create() turns that graph into an Express application. That separation is what lets the same AppModule be started as an HTTP server, as a microservice, or as a bare application context in a CLI script. Delete app.controller.ts, app.service.ts and their specs the moment you add a real feature. They are scaffolding, and leaving them means every reader has to work out that AppService.getHello() is not part of the system. Feature-first, not layer-first Group by the thing that changes together. A change to orders touches the orders controller, the orders service, the orders DTOs and the orders module — put them in one directory. The alternative — src/controllers/, src/services/, src/repositories/ — puts every feature's pieces in different folders. One change edits three directories, each directory eventually holds forty files, and nothing tells you which of those forty belong together. The same argument, made without a framework, is in Layered architecture. src/common/ earns its place only for code with no feature. A @CurrentUser() decorator, a global exception filter, a TransformInterceptor — those belong there. A guard that reads an orders-specific claim belongs in orders/. The layering rules still apply Nest gives you classes and a container. It does not stop you writing a controller that opens a database connection. The rules from Part 1 carry over unchanged, and they are the difference between a Nest app and a Nest-shaped Express app. Layer Owns Must never contain Controller route paths, reading the request, choosing the status code, shaping the response business rules, queries, ORM calls Service business rules, orchestration, transaction boundaries, domain errors Request, Response, HTTP status codes Repository queries, mapping rows to objects business rules, HTTP concepts No Request or Response in a service. In Express the rule is "do not pass req down". In Nest it has an extra edge: injecting @Inject(REQUEST) into a service make

pages.title: Modules
pages.description: How @Module organizes a Nest application into an encapsulated graph — imports, controllers, providers and exports, shared modules, global modules and the cycles to avoid.
headings: One instance per token, per graph
pages.text: A module is a class with a @Module() decorator that declares four things: which other modules it needs, which controllers it owns, which providers it can construct, and which of those providers other modules are allowed to see. That last one is the part people skip, and it is the whole point — Nest's container is encapsulated, so a provider you did not export does not exist outside its own module. Why it exists ES modules already tell you what a file imports. What they cannot tell you is what the runtime graph looks like: which instance of PrismaService the orders service got, whether the payments code is allowed to reach it, and what has to be constructed before the server starts listening. @Module() answers those. It gives the container a boundary it can enforce, which buys you three things: A visible dependency graph. imports on one feature lists exactly which other features it is coupled to. Grep for OrdersModule and you have the complete list of its consumers. Enforced privacy. A repository that is not in exports cannot be injected from another feature, so "just query it from here" is a compile-and-boot-time failure rather than a code review argument. One substitution point. Swapping an implementation for a test, or for a different environment, is a change to one module's providers array rather than to every consumer. The four keys Key Holds Meaning imports modules (or dynamic modules) "I may inject anything these modules export" controllers controller classes "instantiate these and register their routes" providers providers "these are constructible here, and private by default" exports a subset of providers, or a re-exported module "other modules that import me may inject these" OrdersRepository is in providers but not in exports. OrdersService can inject it; PaymentsService cannot, no matter what it imports. That is the encapsulation boundary, and it is worth using deliberately rather than exporting everything out of habit. How resolution actually works When Nest resolves a constructor parameter it looks in exactly two places, in this order: The providers of the module that owns the class doing the injecting. The exports of every module in that module's imports array. It does not search globally, and it does not follow your ES import statements. This is why the most common Nest error is not a missing file: Read it as three questions. Is PaymentsServic

pages.title: Controllers
pages.description: Writing Nest 12 controllers that stay thin — route decorators, parameter decorators, status codes, what Nest does with your return value, and why @Res() is usually a mistake.
headings: What Nest does with your return value
pages.text: A controller is a class whose methods are HTTP endpoints. Its entire job is translation: turn a request into plain values, hand them to one service call, and turn the result into a status code and a body. Everything a controller does beyond that — a query, a rule, a retry, a transaction — is a decision that belongs one layer down. Why it exists Nest could have let you register handler functions directly. The class exists so that a handler can have dependencies resolved by the container, and so that route metadata lives next to the code it routes to instead of in a separate routing table that drifts. That is the trade. You get injectable handlers and colocated routes; you give up the ability to read the whole URL space by opening one file. nest start logs every mapped route at boot, which is the replacement for that file — read it once after adding a controller. Basic example Four endpoints, no req, no res, no try/catch, no status codes except the one that is not a default. Every method is a function from values to values, which is exactly what makes the class testable without a socket. Route decorators @Controller(prefix) sets a path prefix; the method decorator sets the rest. The resulting path is the prefix joined to the method path. Decorator Method Note @Get(path?) GET @Post(path?) POST defaults to 201 @Put(path?) / @Patch(path?) PUT / PATCH @Delete(path?) DELETE @Head(path?) / @Options(path?) HEAD / OPTIONS @All(path?) every method @Search(path?) SEARCH Each accepts string | string[], so one handler can serve several paths: @Controller() also takes an options object with path, host, version and scope. Path syntax — wildcards, optional segments, escaping — is path-to-regexp 8 and has a page of its own: Routing and path syntax. Parameter decorators Nest reads the request for you. Which decorator you use is the difference between a handler that can be unit-tested and one that cannot. Decorator Gives you Express equivalent @Param(key?) a route parameter, or all of them req.params @Query(key?) a query-string value, or all of them req.query @Body(key?) the parsed body, or one property req.body @Headers(name?) one header, or all of them req.headers @Ip() the client IP req.ip @HostParam(key?) a parameter from the host pattern — @Session() the session object req.session @RawBody() the unparsed body buffer requires rawBody: true on the app @Req() / @Res() / @Next

pages.title: Providers and services
pages.description: What a provider is in Nest 12, what belongs in a service versus a repository, and why keeping Request and Response out of the lower layers is both a design rule and a performance one.
headings: No Request or Response below the controller
Services throw, they do not choose status codes
pages.text: A provider is anything the container can construct and hand to something else: a service, a repository, a factory, a configuration object, a third-party client. A service is the most common kind — a class holding business rules, marked @Injectable() and listed in a module's providers array. The distinction matters because "provider" is a container concept and "service" is an architecture one, and confusing them is how you end up with HTTP status codes inside a pricing calculation. Why it exists The service layer is where a rule can live without knowing how it was triggered. An order can be placed by an HTTP request, by a queue consumer replaying a failed job, by a CLI backfill, or by a test. All four need the same rule; only one of them has a Request object. Nest does not enforce this. It gives you classes and a container, and a controller that opens a database connection compiles and runs perfectly. The discipline is yours, and it is the entire difference between a Nest application and an Express application wearing decorators. @Injectable() and the providers array Two things make a class usable by the container, and you need both. @Injectable() marks the class as something whose own constructor dependencies should be resolved. The providers entry registers it under a token — by default, the class itself. A class with @Injectable() that no module lists does not exist to the container; a class in providers without @Injectable() can be constructed only if it has no dependencies, and fails at bootstrap if it has any. Note The constructor above assigns the field explicitly instead of using the constructor(private readonly repository: OrdersRepository) shorthand. Nest treats them identically. The longer form is used throughout this section because parameter properties are not erasable TypeScript syntax — see Native TypeScript support. Use whichever your project's build supports; nothing in Nest depends on the choice. What goes in which class Class Owns Must never contain Controller route paths, reading the request, status codes, response shape business rules, queries, ORM calls Service business rules, orchestration, transaction boundaries, domain errors Request, Response, header names, res.status Repository queries, mapping rows to domain objects, database specifics business rules, HTTP concepts Two prohibitions carry the weight. No Request or Response below the

pages.title: Dependency injection
pages.description: How Nest 12's container resolves constructor parameters — provider tokens, useClass, useValue, useFactory and useExisting, @Inject, optional providers, and breaking circular dependencies with forwardRef.
headings: Injecting into things that are not services
pages.text: Dependency injection is the one feature everything else in Nest is built on. Guards, interceptors, pipes and filters can be classes with their own dependencies because a container exists to resolve them; @nestjs/config, @nestjs/typeorm and @nestjs/jwt are each "a module that provides a token"; and testing works because a token can be pointed at something else. Understanding tokens and provider forms is therefore not advanced material — it is the thing that makes the error messages readable. Why it exists The alternative is a composition root: one file that constructs everything in order and passes it down. That is a perfectly good design, and the plain-Express chapter uses it. What a container buys you over it is transitivity. In a manual composition root, adding a dependency to a leaf service means editing the factory call for that service, and the factory call for everything that constructs it, and so on up. Nest resolves the whole graph from constructor types, so adding a dependency three levels down changes exactly one constructor. What you give up is a greppable wiring file. The wiring is now distributed across @Module() decorators, and the compiler cannot tell you that a token is unresolvable — bootstrap does, which is early but not as early as a type error. Constructor injection Nest reads the constructor's parameter types and resolves each one. That is the whole mechanism for the common case. The parameter type is the token here, which is why this only works for classes. TypeScript erases interfaces, so constructor(repo: IOrdersRepository) has nothing to resolve at runtime — the metadata the container reads would say Object. When you want to depend on an abstraction, use an abstract class or an explicit token with @Inject(). Note This reflection depends on emitDecoratorMetadata and reflect-metadata (0.2.2), which is why Nest projects always have a real tsc build step and cannot run under Node's type stripping. See Native TypeScript support. Tokens Every provider is registered under a token. The token is what the container looks up; the class is just the default token for a class provider. Token kind Written as Use it when Class OrdersService the common case — one implementation, resolved by type string 'DATABASEPOOL' quick, greppable, and collides silently across packages symbol Symbol('DATABASEPOOL') the safe version of the above — cannot collide Ab

pages.title: Injection scopes
pages.description: DEFAULT, REQUEST and TRANSIENT in Nest 12 — what each means, why request scope bubbles up the whole injector chain, and how durable providers limit the damage.
headings: Why DEFAULT is right almost always
The alternatives, in order of preference
Finding out what is actually scoped
pages.text: By default every provider in Nest is a singleton: constructed once at bootstrap and shared by everything that injects it. Two other scopes exist, and the second one — REQUEST — is the single most expensive decision available in the framework, because it is contagious. Setting it on one leaf provider can convert half your application into per-request construction, and the only symptom is that throughput quietly drops. The three scopes Scope Instances Constructed Use for Scope.DEFAULT one, application-wide at bootstrap everything, unless you have a specific reason Scope.REQUEST one per request pipeline on each request genuinely per-request state you cannot pass as an argument Scope.TRANSIENT one per injecting class when each consumer is constructed a provider that must not share state between consumers Scope can also be set on a custom provider ({ provide: X, useClass: Y, scope: Scope.REQUEST }), on a controller (@Controller({ path: 'orders', scope: Scope.REQUEST })), and on guards, interceptors, pipes and filters. Why DEFAULT is right almost always A singleton is constructed once, so per-request cost is zero, and it can hold things that are expensive to create and safe to share: a connection pool, a compiled schema, an in-memory cache, an HTTP client with keep-alive. It is also the reason the boot-time failure mode exists. Every singleton is instantiated during NestFactory.create(), so a provider whose constructor or onModuleInit throws takes the process down before it listens. That is what you want — the container proves the graph is constructible before accepting traffic. The one rule a singleton imposes: no per-request state on this. A field assigned during one request is visible to every concurrent request. If a provider needs a value that varies per request, it takes it as a method argument. What REQUEST scope actually costs The cost is not "one extra object per request". It is that request scope bubbles up the injector chain. When a provider is request-scoped, any provider that injects it must also be constructed per request — it cannot be a singleton holding a reference to something that does not exist yet. That propagates transitively, all the way up to the controller. Now every request constructs four objects instead of zero, and each construction walks its own dependency list. Three consequences, in order of how much they usually hurt: Per-request i

pages.title: The request lifecycle
pages.description: The exact order a Nest 12 request passes through — middleware, guards, interceptors, pipes, handler, interceptors again, exception filters — where each stage can short-circuit, and where async errors surface.
headings: Why the order is what it is
Where each stage can stop the request
Exception filters are the last stage, always
What runs when nothing matches a route
pages.text: Every request through a Nest application walks the same fixed pipeline. Knowing the order is not trivia: it decides where authentication can read a parsed body, why a pipe cannot reject a request before a guard has run, and which stage an error was thrown from when a filter finally sees it. This page is the reference the rest of the NestJS sections point back to. The order # Stage Sees Can short-circuit by Typical job 1 Middleware raw req, res, next responding, or next(err) request id, body parsing, CORS, helmet, logging 2 Guards ExecutionContext returning false, or throwing authentication, authorization, rate limits 3 Interceptors (pre) ExecutionContext, CallHandler not calling next.handle(), or throwing caching, timing, starting a span 4 Pipes one argument + its metadata throwing parsing, coercion, DTO validation 5 Handler the resolved arguments throwing one service call 6 Interceptors (post) the result stream mapping to a different value, or throwing serialization, envelopes, timeouts 7 Exception filters the exception + ArgumentsHost always terminal turning an error into a response Within each enhancer stage, registration scope decides order: global → controller → route handler. So a global guard runs before a @UseGuards() on the controller, which runs before a @UseGuards() on the method. Note Interceptors are the only stage that runs twice. Everything before return next.handle() executes on the way in, at position 3; the RxJS operators you .pipe() onto that stream execute on the way out, at position 6, after the handler has resolved. Why the order is what it is Three of the adjacencies do real work, and they are the ones worth internalizing. Middleware before guards. Middleware is Express's stack, running before Nest's routing has resolved which handler will serve the request. That is why middleware cannot know the controller or method it is running for, and why a guard — which receives an ExecutionContext carrying both — is the right place for anything that depends on route metadata. It is also why body parsing has to be middleware: a guard that reads request.body needs it already parsed. Guards before interceptors. Rejecting an unauthenticated request should not first allocate a cache key, open a tracing span or start a timer. Guards are the cheap, terminal stage. Guards before pipes. This one bites people. pages.description: How Nest 12 compiles route decorators with path-to-regexp 8 on Express 5 — wildcards, optional segments, arrays of paths, escaping, route ordering, and the new route-conflict diagnostics.
headings: The errors you will actually see
pages.text: @nestjs/platform-express@12.0.1 bundles express@5.2.1 and path-to-regexp@8.4.2, so the string inside @Get() is compiled by exactly the same matcher as a plain Express 5 route. Every path rule from Part 1 applies here unchanged — and the patterns that Express 4 accepted now throw a TypeError at bootstrap rather than failing at request time. Nest 12 also ships opt-in diagnostics that tell you when two routes collide, which is the first framework-level answer to a class of bug that used to be silent. The underlying grammar The mechanics of path-to-regexp 8 — parameter names, wildcards, optional groups, escaping, what req.params contains — are covered once in Route parameters and path syntax. Read that page for the grammar. This page covers the decorator forms and what Nest adds on top. The short version: Construct Meaning Nest example Matches :name one segment, captured @Get('books/:id') /books/42 name one or more segments, captured as an array @Get('files/path') /files/a/b.txt { … } an optional group @Get('books{/:id}') /books and /books/42 | escape the next character | @Get('reports/\(draft\)') | /reports/(draft)` (, ), [, ], ?, + and ! are reserved. Used literally they throw; escape them with a backslash (doubled in a TypeScript string literal). The decorator forms Catch-all routes The braces are the whole difference, and getting it wrong is a subtle bug: with the unbraced form, every URL works except /. For a single-page-app fallback or a 404 handler you want '{splat}'. req.params.splat is an array of segments, not a slash-joined string. Read it with @Param('splat') and join it yourself when you need a path — and never hand the joined value to the filesystem without resolving it against a root and checking containment. Optional segments and file extensions There are no ?, + or suffix modifiers any more. Optionality is a group. The group is the whole optional unit — the . and the :ext together. An unmatched parameter is omitted from req.params entirely rather than present as undefined, so 'ext' in request.params and Object.keys() behave differently than they did on Express 4. Several paths for one handler Regex-in-a-string is gone. Every route decorator accepts string | string[], so pass an array: This is checked at bootstrap, reads better than an alternation, and is what @Controller({ path: ['v1', 'v2'] }) does at the prefix level too. Note Nest's route dec

pages.title: Configuration
pages.description: Using @nestjs/config 12.0.0 — ConfigModule.forRoot, typed ConfigService.get, namespaced config with registerAs, and boot-time validation with a Standard Schema or Joi v18.
pages.text: @nestjs/config is 12.0.0, and the headline change in this line is that validationSchema now accepts any Standard Schema — a Zod 4, Valibot or ArkType schema works directly, with no adapter. The job of the module has not changed: read the environment once, validate it at boot, and hand the rest of the application typed values instead of process.env lookups scattered across forty files. Why it exists process.env.DATABASEURL works. It is also a string | undefined that can be misspelled with no error, that reads as undefined in a worker that loaded a different .env, and that fails on the first request rather than at startup. A config module fixes three specific things: Fail fast. A missing or malformed variable kills the process at boot, before the orchestrator routes traffic to it. A config error at 09:00 on deploy is an incident; the same error at 03:00 under load is an outage. One source of truth. Everything reads ConfigService, so "what does this service need in its environment" is answerable by reading one file. A substitution seam. ConfigService is a provider, so a test overrides it like any other token — no process.env mutation, no cross-test leakage. Setup Option Effect isGlobal registers the module globally so features do not each import it cache caches process.env reads in memory — measurably faster, and correct because the environment does not change at runtime envFilePath one path or an ordered list; the first file that defines a key wins load factory functions returning nested config objects expandVariables enables dotenv-expand, so URL=${HOST}:${PORT} resolves ignoreEnvFile skip .env entirely — what you want in a container that gets real environment variables validationSchema a Standard Schema validated at boot validationOptions options passed to that schema's validation validate a plain function alternative to a schema validatePredefined whether variables already in process.env at import time are validated (default true) skipProcessEnv make ConfigService.get ignore process.env and read only loaded config (default false) isGlobal: true is the one genuinely justified @Global() in most applications — configuration really is needed everywhere, and the alternative is ConfigModule in every feature's imports. Everything narrower should be a normal shared module; see Modules. Note envFilePath order is "first definition wins", which is the opposite of what

pages.title: ESM vs CommonJS
pages.description: NestJS 12 core packages ship as ES modules — what that changes for CommonJS apps (almost nothing), how to opt into ESM properly, what breaks, and how to choose.
headings: 5. Check what the rest of the project assumed
Bundler configurations that assume CJS-only packages
pages.text: The headline change in the NestJS 12 line is that @nestjs/core and @nestjs/common both declare "type": "module" and their internal imports carry .js extensions. That sounds like a migration and mostly is not one: CommonJS applications consume the ESM packages through require(esm) with no rewrite at all, and nest upgrade deliberately preserves whatever module format your project already uses. This page is about the decision you now get to make, not one you are forced into. What actually changed Nest 11 Nest 12 @nestjs/core, @nestjs/common on disk CommonJS ESM ("type": "module") A CommonJS app consuming them require() require(esm) — same source, no change An ESM app consuming them interop through the CJS build native ESM, real named exports nest upgrade — keeps the project's existing format nest new defaults CommonJS + Jest + ESLint ESM projects default to Vitest; generated projects default to oxlint require(esm) is the Node feature that makes this a non-event. A CommonJS file can require() an ES module synchronously, provided the module graph has no top-level await. Nest's packages are built with that constraint in mind, which is why a Nest 11 CommonJS application upgrades to 12 without touching a single import statement. The Node-level mechanics — the resolution algorithm, exports maps, dual-package hazards, why require(esm) works and when it does not — are covered once in ESM vs CommonJS. Read that page for the platform behavior; this one covers what Nest adds. Note Running a Nest 12 app needs Node v20.19+, v22.12+, or v26+, which are the versions where require(esm) is available. The CLI needs more: v22.22.3+, v24.15+, or v26+, because @nestjs/schematics@12.0.0 declares >=22.12.0. This handbook targets Node 24 LTS, which satisfies both. Staying on CommonJS Nothing to do. Keep "type" out of package.json (or set it to "commonjs"), keep module: "commonjs" in tsconfig.json, keep your imports without extensions, keep dirname. This is the right choice for most existing applications, and it is not a deprecated path — it is the format the CLI preserves on upgrade and the one the majority of the ecosystem still ships. The reasons to stay: Zero migration cost. The alternative touches every relative import in the repository. Bundlers and tooling that assume CJS-only packages keep working. Jest works without the experimental-VM-modules dance. dirname and require.resolv

pages.title: Middleware
pages.description: Functional and class middleware in NestJS 12, binding them with MiddlewareConsumer, and why middleware runs before guards and never sees the ExecutionContext.
headings: Path syntax is Express 5 path syntax
Capturing a raw body for webhook signatures
pages.text: Middleware in Nest is Express middleware: a (req, res, next) function that runs before the route handler is even selected. It is the only stage of the Nest pipeline that is not Nest-aware — it gets the raw platform request and nothing else. That limitation is the whole reason guards, interceptors and pipes exist. Why it exists Nest keeps middleware because the Express ecosystem is full of useful (req, res, next) functions — helmet(), cookie-parser, a raw-body capture for webhook signatures — and rewriting them as guards would be pointless. Middleware is the adapter layer for that ecosystem, plus the right place for work that must happen before routing. Everything that needs to know which handler is about to run belongs one stage later. See The request lifecycle for the full order. Where it sits Nest runs enhancers in a fixed order. Middleware is first: Stage Sees the request Sees the target handler Can short-circuit Middleware yes (raw req/res) no yes, by responding or next(err) Guards yes, via ExecutionContext yes yes, by returning false or throwing Interceptors (before) yes, via ExecutionContext yes yes, by returning its own observable Pipes the bound argument only yes yes, by throwing Handler yes — — The consequence that trips people up: middleware runs before guards, always. A middleware cannot read metadata set with @SetMetadata() or Reflector.createDecorator(), cannot call context.getHandler(), and cannot know whether the route it is running for is public or protected — because at that point Nest has not chosen a handler. Warning If you find yourself wanting ExecutionContext inside middleware, you want a guard or an interceptor. There is no supported way to get one; use() receives only the platform req, res and next. Basic example A functional middleware is a plain function. It is the right default when the middleware has no dependencies. A class middleware implements NestMiddleware and participates in dependency injection, so it can take providers in its constructor. Note private readonly logger = new Logger(...) is a class field, not a constructor parameter property. Nest examples across this handbook avoid parameter properties (constructor(private readonly x: X) {}) because Node's type-stripping cannot compile them, and the site lints every snippet by stripping it. Injected dependencies are declared as a field and assigned in the constructor body —

pages.title: Guards
pages.description: CanActivate, ExecutionContext and Reflector in NestJS 12 — binding guards at three scopes, returning false versus throwing, and why a guard cannot do object-level authorization.
headings: Guards are the wrong place for object-level authorization
Opting a route out of a global guard
Getting a value out of a guard
pages.text: A guard is a class with one method that answers a single yes/no question before the handler runs: may this request proceed? It is the first stage of the pipeline that knows which controller and which method are about to be invoked, which is what makes it the right home for authentication and role checks — and what makes it useless for anything that depends on the resource itself. Why it exists Middleware runs before Nest has resolved a route, so it cannot read route metadata. Guards run after resolution and receive an ExecutionContext carrying both getClass() and getHandler(). That is the entire difference, and it is the reason @Roles('admin') on a controller method can be enforced at all. Guards are also the cheapest terminal stage. Rejecting a request in a guard happens before interceptors allocate anything, before pipes parse a body, and before a single line of your service runs. See The request lifecycle for where that sits relative to everything else. Basic example canActivate() may return boolean, Promise<boolean> or Observable<boolean>. Nest awaits or subscribes as needed, so an async guard needs no special registration. The ExecutionContext ExecutionContext extends ArgumentsHost with two methods that only exist because routing has already happened. Method Returns Used for context.getHandler() the method that will be called metadata set by a method decorator context.getClass() the controller class metadata set by a class decorator context.switchToHttp().getRequest() the Express Request headers, cookies, request.params context.switchToHttp().getResponse() the Express Response setting a header before rejection context.getType() 'http', 'ws' or 'rpc' writing one guard for HTTP and microservices getRequest() and getResponse() are generic, so type them: getRequest<Request>(). Untyped, everything downstream is any and a typo in a header name becomes a silent undefined. Note A guard shared between HTTP controllers and microservice handlers must branch on context.getType() before calling switchToHttp() — the HTTP host is not populated for an RPC context, and you will read undefined rather than get an error. Binding guards Three scopes, and they run global first, then controller, then handler. @UseGuards() takes classes or instances. Pass the class whenever the guard has dependencies — Nest instantiates it through the container and injects them. An instance yo

pages.title: Interceptors
pages.description: NestInterceptor and CallHandler in NestJS 12 — the RxJS operators that shape responses, add timing, caching and timeouts, and how StreamableFile leaves the pipeline.
headings: Caching: returning without calling the handler
Streaming a file out of the pipeline
pages.text: An interceptor is the only stage of the Nest pipeline that runs on both sides of the handler. Everything before return next.handle() executes on the way in; the RxJS operators you attach to that stream execute on the way out, after the handler has resolved. That gives you one class that can time a request, wrap its response, retry it, cancel it, or replace it entirely without ever calling the handler. Why it exists Guards answer yes or no. Pipes transform one argument. Filters only see failures. Nothing else in the pipeline can observe a successful response — and response shaping, timing, caching and serialization all need exactly that. The mechanism is RxJS. next.handle() returns an Observable of whatever the handler produced (a promise is awaited first, so you see the resolved value), and your intercept() returns an Observable that Nest subscribes to. See The request lifecycle for positions 3 and 6. Basic example The tap({ next, error }) form matters: a bare tap(fn) only fires on success, so a failing handler would never be timed. An interceptor that only measures the happy path hides exactly the requests you care about. The contract Three rules follow from those signatures: intercept() may be async. Returning Promise<Observable<T>> is supported, which lets you await a cache lookup before deciding whether to call the handler. The handler does not run until the returned observable is subscribed to. next.handle() is lazy. Not calling it — or never subscribing to it — skips pipes and the handler entirely. You may call next.handle() exactly once per request. Subscribing twice invokes the handler twice. ExecutionContext is the same object a guard gets, with getClass(), getHandler() and switchToHttp(). See Guards for the full surface. Binding interceptors Binding Dependency injection Scope @UseInterceptors(Class) yes controller or handler @UseInterceptors(new Class()) no controller or handler APPINTERCEPTOR provider yes every route app.useGlobalInterceptors(new Class()) no every route Ordering is the part people get wrong. Registration scope decides the entry order — global, then controller, then handler — and because interceptors nest, the exit order is the reverse. A global logging interceptor therefore wraps the response that a handler-level envelope interceptor produced, not the other way around. Note A global interceptor never runs for a request that matche

pages.title: Pipes
pages.description: The built-in parse pipes in NestJS 12, writing a PipeTransform, ArgumentMetadata, and binding pipes at parameter, handler and global scope.
headings: Validation belongs on its own page
Pipes do not see the whole request
pages.text: A pipe is a class with one method that receives a single handler argument and returns the value the handler will actually get. It does two jobs that are really one: turn the string a client sent into the type your code expects, and reject it if it cannot. Everything a pipe touches is one argument — it never sees the request as a whole. Why it exists Route parameters, query strings and headers are always strings. @Param('id') id: number is a lie that TypeScript cannot catch, because types are erased before the request arrives. A pipe is the runtime half of that annotation. The second job follows from the first: a conversion that can fail is a validation. ParseIntPipe throws a 400 for ?page=banana for the same reason it returns a number for ?page=2. Pipes run at position 4, after guards and interceptors and immediately before the handler. That ordering is deliberate — see The request lifecycle — and it is why a request with both a bad token and a malformed body returns 403 rather than 400. Built-in pipes All of these live in @nestjs/common. Pipe Turns Into Throws ParseIntPipe '42' 42 400 on a non-integer ParseFloatPipe '1.5' 1.5 400 on a non-number ParseBoolPipe 'true' / 'false' true / false 400 on anything else ParseArrayPipe 'a,b,c' or an array body an array, optionally of DTOs 400 per invalid item ParseEnumPipe 'ACTIVE' the enum member 400 when not a member ParseUUIDPipe a UUID string the same string, validated 400 on a malformed UUID ParseDatePipe a date string a Date 400 on an unparseable date DefaultValuePipe undefined the default you supplied never ParseFilePipe an uploaded file the same file, validated 400 (configurable) ValidationPipe a plain object a validated DTO instance 400 with the error list StandardSchemaValidationPipe a plain value the schema's output 400 with the schema issues Pipes listed on one parameter run left to right, which is why DefaultValuePipe comes first: it substitutes the default before ParseIntPipe sees undefined. Shared options Most parse pipes accept the same three options, verified against the 12.0.1 declarations: Option Effect optional return null/undefined unchanged instead of throwing (default false) errorHttpStatusCode the status to throw instead of 400 exceptionFactory build the exception yourself from the error string Returning 404 rather than 400 for a non-numeric id is a small but real improvement: /users/banana is n

pages.title: Exception filters
pages.description: The built-in exception layer in NestJS 12, HttpException and its subclasses, writing a @Catch() filter, and building a stable machine-readable error contract with the v12 errorCode option.
pages.text: Nest wraps every request in an exception layer. Anything thrown by a guard, an interceptor, a pipe or a handler is caught by the framework, matched against your filters, and turned into a response — you never write try/catch to convert an error into a status code. This page is about controlling what that response says. The built-in layer Without a single filter of your own, Nest already handles two cases. An HttpException becomes its declared status and body: Anything else becomes a generic 500 and is logged: That second behavior is the important one: an unrecognized exception never leaks its message to the client. The string is exactly Internal server error, and the real error goes to the ExceptionsHandler logger instead. Any filter you write has to preserve that property. Note HttpException extends IntrinsicException, and the built-in handler does not log those — a 404 you threw on purpose is not an error in your logs. Unknown exceptions are logged in full. If you replace the default handling with your own global filter, you inherit the responsibility for that distinction. HttpException and its subclasses HttpExceptionOptions in Nest 12, read from the published declarations: The subclasses fill in the status for you, and all of them take the same options object as their second argument. Exception Status Exception Status BadRequestException 400 PayloadTooLargeException 413 UnauthorizedException 401 UnsupportedMediaTypeException 415 ForbiddenException 403 UnprocessableEntityException 422 NotFoundException 404 InternalServerErrorException 500 MethodNotAllowedException 405 NotImplementedException 501 NotAcceptableException 406 BadGatewayException 502 RequestTimeoutException 408 ServiceUnavailableException 503 ConflictException 409 GatewayTimeoutException 504 GoneException 410 HttpVersionNotSupportedException 505 PreconditionFailedException 412 MisdirectedException 421 ImATeapotException 418 Use HttpStatus from @nestjs/common rather than a bare number when you construct HttpException directly. cause cause is the standard Error chaining field, and it is how you keep the original failure without putting it in the response. The client sees Payment provider unavailable. Your logs see the gateway's stack trace, hanging off exception.cause. pages.title: Custom decorators
pages.description: createParamDecorator and applyDecorators in NestJS 12, metadata decorators with SetMetadata and Reflector.createDecorator, and why validation skips custom parameters by default.
headings: Passing pipes to a custom decorator
Validation skips custom parameters by default
pages.text: Nest's decorators are ordinary functions that attach metadata, and you can write your own. Three kinds are worth building: a parameter decorator that extracts a value from the request, a metadata decorator that a guard or interceptor reads back, and a composite decorator that bundles several existing ones into one line. Why it exists request.user is set by an authentication guard and read by every handler that needs it. Without a decorator that means @Req() request: Request in forty signatures, an any cast, and a coupling to Express that makes the controller untestable without a fake request object. A custom decorator moves that knowledge into one file. The controller says what it wants, not where it lives. Parameter decorators The factory signature is (data, context) => value. data is whatever the caller passed to the decorator — 'id' above, undefined when it is called bare — and context is the same ExecutionContext a guard gets, so getHandler(), getClass() and getType() are all available. Warning request.user is populated by a guard. A custom decorator that reads it runs after guards, so on a route with no authentication guard the value is undefined and the handler receives undefined rather than an error. Make the decorator return undefined honestly (as above) and let the guard be the thing that enforces presence — a decorator that throws when the user is missing hides a missing @UseGuards(). Other things worth extracting Danger request.ip and X-Forwarded-For are attacker-controlled unless trust proxy is set to the exact number of proxies in front of you. A rate limiter or an audit log keyed on a spoofable client IP is worse than one with no IP at all, because it looks like it works. The Express-level configuration is in Request and response; the abuse case is in Rate limiting and abuse. Passing pipes to a custom decorator The decorator returned by createParamDecorator() accepts pipes after the data argument, exactly like @Param() and @Query() do: The pipe runs on the value the factory produced, not on the raw request. Validation skips custom parameters by default This is the detail that surprises people, and Nest 12 made it explicit in the type declarations. pages.description: Why a NestJS DTO is a class and a security boundary rather than a type, composing them with @nestjs/mapped-types 12.0.0, and keeping request and response DTOs apart.
headings: Why a DTO must be a class
A DTO is a security boundary
Type the parameter, but do not trust the type
Request DTOs and response DTOs are different objects
pages.text: A DTO is the class that describes one payload crossing your API boundary. In Nest it is not documentation and not a convenience — it is the runtime artifact that decides which fields of a request survive into your service, which is why it has to be a class and why getting it wrong is a vulnerability rather than a type error. Why a DTO must be a class TypeScript types are erased at compile time. An interface CreateUserDto leaves nothing behind for ValidationPipe to inspect, so ArgumentMetadata.metatype is Object and validation silently does nothing — the request passes, unvalidated, and every test still goes green. A class survives compilation, carries class-validator metadata via reflect-metadata, and is what ValidationPipe reflects over. The decorators are class-validator 0.15.1; the transformation half is class-transformer 0.5.1. Both are optional peer dependencies of @nestjs/common@12.0.1, so you install them yourself. The alternative stack — a Zod schema through StandardSchemaValidationPipe — is covered in Standard Schema with Zod; the class form is what the rest of this page assumes. Note A DTO class is inert without a ValidationPipe. Declaring @IsEmail() and never registering the pipe produces a DTO that documents a rule nobody enforces. Register it once globally through APPPIPE — see Pipes. A DTO is a security boundary The important property of a DTO is not the fields it declares. It is the fields it excludes. If users.create() passes that object to an ORM, the caller just granted themselves admin and skipped email verification. That is mass assignment, and the DTO is the control that stops it — but only with the right pipe options: Option Without it With it whitelist: true every extra property reaches your service only decorated properties survive forbidNonWhitelisted: true extras are dropped quietly a 400 naming the unexpected property transform: true the handler gets a plain object the handler gets a CreateUserDto instance whitelist is the one that matters. Without it, the DTO declares a shape and enforces nothing about what else came along. forbidNonWhitelisted turns a silent strip into a loud failure, which is what you want in development and usually in production too — a client sending fields you do not accept has a bug you would rather hear about. pages.title: Versioning
pages.description: app.enableVersioning() in NestJS 12 with URI, header, media-type and custom strategies, per-controller versions, VERSION_NEUTRAL, and an honest look at what versioning costs.
headings: How it interacts with everything else
When versioning is worth the cost
Sharing the service layer, not the controller
pages.text: Nest can route the same path to different handlers based on a version the client asks for. Four strategies ship in the box, they are configured in one call, and the decorators are trivial. The hard part is not the mechanism — it is deciding whether you need it at all, because every version you publish is a version you maintain. Enabling it enableVersioning() called with no arguments defaults to { type: VersioningType.URI }. defaultVersion is shared by all four strategies and applies to any controller or handler that declares no version of its own — without it, an unversioned handler is unreachable once versioning is on. The four strategies Type Client sends Options Cacheable by URL VersioningType.URI /v1/users prefix?: string | false (default 'v') yes VersioningType.HEADER a request header header: string only with Vary VersioningType.MEDIATYPE Accept: application/json;v=1 key: string (e.g. 'v=') only with Vary VersioningType.CUSTOM anything you can read off the request extractor: (request) => string | string[] depends CUSTOM's extractor returning an array is the interesting case: Nest tries each version in order, so ['2', '1'] means "give me v2 if this route has one, otherwise fall back to v1". The declaration order is highest to lowest — reversing it silently pins every client to your oldest handler. URI is the right default. It is visible in logs and in a proxy's access log, it caches without Vary, it is trivial to curl, and a client can bookmark it. Header and media-type versioning are cleaner in theory — the resource identifier does not change — and in practice they make every debugging session harder and every CDN configuration more fragile. Warning With HEADER or MEDIATYPE versioning, two versions of a resource share one URL. Any cache in front of your API will serve one version's response to a client asking for the other unless you set Vary on the version header. That includes browser caches, your CDN, and any reverse proxy with a default cache config. Declaring versions @Version() is a method decorator. Controller-level versions go through the @Controller() options object. Both controllers are registered in the module as normal. Nest routes /v1/users to the first and /v2/users to the second. A single handler can serve several versions, and a method-level @Version() overrides the controller's: Versions are strings, always. version: 1 is a type error,
