pages.description: Multipart uploads in NestJS 12 with the bundled multer 2.2.0 — the four file interceptors, multer limits, ParseFilePipe validators, and a custom validator that sniffs magic bytes.
headings: limits — every default that matters is unbounded
ParseFilePipe and FileFieldsInterceptor do not mix
A custom validator that sniffs the real bytes
Never let the client name the file
fileFilter rejects a part before its bytes arrive
Large files: take your server off the data path
pages.text: An upload endpoint lets an anonymous caller write bytes to your infrastructure and usually hands back a URL that serves those bytes again. Nest wraps multer in four interceptors and gives you ParseFilePipe to validate what arrives, but every decision that matters — how large, what type, where it lands, who can read it back — is still yours. What is already installed @nestjs/platform-express@12.0.1 depends on multer@2.2.0. You do not install multer, and you do not add @types/multer-driven middleware by hand; the interceptors below are the supported surface. Deprecated multer 1.x is end of life and deprecated on npm. The final 1.x release, 1.4.5-lts.2, carries the registry deprecation notice "Multer 1.x is impacted by a number of vulnerabilities, which have been patched in 2.x." There is no supported 1.x line and no backport branch. Nest 12 pins 2.2.0, so a fresh project is fine. Run npm ls multer anyway — a transitive 1.x from some other package is the case that bites, and the advisories apply to it just the same. Nest also depends on file-type@22.0.2 in @nestjs/common@12.0.1, which is what makes the built-in FileTypeValidator able to check magic numbers rather than trusting the client. That is new enough to be worth saying out loud: in Nest 12 the built-in type validator is a real content check by default. Note multer@2.2.0 ships no type declarations, so the Express.Multer.File type used throughout this page needs the ambient definitions: It is a dev dependency — nothing about it reaches the runtime — and @types/multer is at 2.2.0, matching the bundled multer. The four interceptors All four come from @nestjs/platform-express and are functions returning an interceptor class. Interceptor Signature Handler reads FileInterceptor (fieldName, localOptions?) @UploadedFile() → one file FilesInterceptor (fieldName, maxCount?, localOptions?) @UploadedFiles() → an array FileFieldsInterceptor (uploadFields: MulterField[], localOptions?) @UploadedFiles() → a record keyed by field name AnyFilesInterceptor (localOptions?) @UploadedFiles() → an array of every file on every field There is a fifth, NoFilesInterceptor(localOptions?), which parses a multipart form's text fields and rejects any file. It is the right choice for a form that is multipart only because a browser made it so. MulterField is { name: string; maxCount?: number }. Declare maxCount on every field — omitting

pages.title: The ValidationPipe
pages.description: How the classic NestJS ValidationPipe works, every option that matters, and why it belongs at the global level rather than on individual handlers.
headings: Why global is the default answer
The skip options are sharper than they look
pages.text: ValidationPipe is the piece of NestJS that turns a DTO class into an enforced contract. It takes the raw value a parameter decorator produced, hands it to class-transformer and class-validator, and either passes a typed instance to your handler or throws a BadRequestException before your handler ever runs. NestJS 12 ships two validation stacks. This page is about the classic one. The Standard Schema alternative is on Standard Schema with Zod, and Choosing an approach compares them. Why it exists Without a pipe, @Body() gives you whatever express.json() parsed — a plain object with no guarantees. The CreateUserDto type annotation on the parameter is erased at compile time and enforces nothing at runtime. ValidationPipe closes that gap. It is the only reason the DTO class means anything at runtime. Installation class-validator and class-transformer are peer dependencies of @nestjs/common — Nest does not bundle them, and ValidationPipe throws a descriptive error at first use if they are missing. Verified versions: class-validator 0.15.1, class-transformer 0.5.1, reflect-metadata 0.2.2. The DTO's types — the difference between email: string and email: number — are only visible at runtime if TypeScript emits them, so the compiler options are load-bearing: Both flags are non-negotiable for this stack; see class-validator and class-transformer for what breaks without them. Basic example A request with a bad email now returns a 400 with a per-field message, and the handler is never entered. Where to bind it There are three places, and they are not equivalent. Globally, from the bootstrap file Simple, and correct for most applications. The limitation is that the pipe is constructed outside the DI container, so it cannot inject providers. Globally, as a provider APPPIPE registers the pipe inside the container, so it can inject a ConfigService or a logger. It also keeps the pipe active in tests that build the app from AppModule without going through main.ts — a common reason validation silently disappears in end-to-end tests. Per handler or per parameter Use these only to override the global pipe for one route. A more local pipe replaces the global one for that parameter — it does not merge with it, so an override that forgets whitelist: true reopens mass assignment on exactly that route. Best practice Bind it globally, once, with whitelist and forbidNonWhitelisted on.

pages.title: class-validator and class-transformer
pages.description: The decorator-based validation stack in NestJS 12 — the common constraints, nested and array validation, custom and async validators, and what a 0.x dependency means for your API.
headings: The constraints you will actually use
pages.text: class-validator 0.15.1 and class-transformer 0.5.1 are the two packages that give a DTO class runtime meaning. ValidationPipe is only the adapter; these libraries do the work. They are peer dependencies of @nestjs/common, so you install and version them yourself. Why it exists A DTO is a class whose properties carry the contract. Constraints live next to the field they constrain, so there is nothing to keep in sync — the type, the validation and the OpenAPI description are all on the same line of the same file. The runtime requirement This stack is built on reflect-metadata 0.2.2 and the TypeScript metadata emit. Both are required. reflect-metadata must be imported once, before anything decorated is loaded: Warning Node's native TypeScript type-stripping (node --experimental-strip-types, unflagged from Node 23.6) cannot run this code. Type-stripping erases types without emitting anything, so emitDecoratorMetadata has nothing to emit and legacy decorators are not executed at all. A NestJS project using class-validator needs a real compile step — nest build, tsc, or a bundler that runs the TypeScript transform. Not an SWC/esbuild configuration with decorator metadata turned off, either. What breaks without emitDecoratorMetadata is subtle rather than loud: @ValidateNested() cannot discover the nested class, so nested objects are not validated. @Type() is what saves you here, which is why it is not optional. class-transformer cannot convert types implicitly, so @Type(() => Number) becomes mandatory everywhere. ValidationPipe may see Object as the metatype and skip the parameter silently. The constraints you will actually use Group Decorators Presence @IsDefined(), @IsNotEmpty(), @IsOptional(), @Allow() Primitives @IsString(), @IsInt(), @IsNumber(), @IsBoolean(), @IsArray(), @IsObject() Numbers @Min(), @Max(), @IsPositive(), @IsNegative() Strings @Length(), @MinLength(), @MaxLength(), @Matches(), @IsNotEmpty() Formats @IsEmail(), @IsUUID(), @IsUrl(), @IsISO8601(), @IsDateString(), @IsJSON() Sets @IsIn(), @IsNotIn(), @IsEnum() Arrays @ArrayMinSize(), @ArrayMaxSize(), @ArrayUnique(), @ArrayNotEmpty() Structure @ValidateNested(), @ValidateIf(), @Validate() Two behaviors are worth memorizing because they cause most of the confusion: @IsOptional() skips every other constraint when the value is null or undefined. It is not "may be absent" — it is "if absent, stop". A f

pages.title: Standard Schema with Zod
pages.description: The schema-first validation stack new in NestJS 12 — StandardSchemaValidationPipe with Zod 4, Valibot or ArkType, attached per parameter and typed with z.infer.
pages.text: NestJS 12 added a second validation stack. StandardSchemaValidationPipe takes a schema from the parameter decorator instead of a DTO class, validates against it, and hands your handler the schema's output. It works with any library that implements the Standard Schema spec — Zod 4.5.4, Valibot 1.4.2 and ArkType 2.2.3 all do. This is the schema-first alternative to the ValidationPipe. It does not replace it; both ship in @nestjs/common 12.0.1 and both can be registered at once. Choosing an approach is the page that argues about which one you should use. Why it exists The classic stack needs a class, decorator metadata, experimentalDecorators, emitDecoratorMetadata, and two pre-1.0 peer dependencies. That is a lot of machinery to say "this body has an email and a display name". A Standard Schema is a plain value. There is no metadata emit, no reflection, no class to construct — the schema carries its own validator under a standard property, and Nest calls it. The type you program against is derived from the schema, so the two cannot drift apart. @standard-schema/spec 1.1.0 is the shared interface. It is a types-only package: the schema libraries implement it, and Nest consumes it. Installation Only the schema library is an actual runtime dependency. @standard-schema/spec ships types, and @nestjs/common already declares it. Nothing in this stack needs reflect-metadata, class-validator, class-transformer, or emitDecoratorMetadata. Nest's own decorators still need experimentalDecorators and a real compile step, so the tsconfig is unchanged from any other Nest project — you just stop depending on metadata emit for validation. Basic example The schema is an ordinary module-level value. Attach it to the parameter with the schema option on @Body(): Then register the pipe once, globally: The path: message prefix is the pipe's own default formatting — it joins each issue's path with . and prefixes the message. There is no field-keyed object in the default body; if you want one, write an exceptionFactory. Best practice Register the pipe globally and attach a schema per parameter. A parameter with no schema is passed straight through untouched, so "forgot the schema" is silent — the same opt-in-security problem a per-route ValidationPipe has. Decide on it once and enforce it in review, or keep the global ValidationPipe alongside as a backstop for class DTOs. Registering i

pages.description: A balanced comparison of class-validator and Standard Schema in NestJS 12 — ergonomics, type-inference direction, runtime cost, Swagger, refactoring safety, and when each is the wrong choice.
headings: Type-inference direction is the real fork
Ecosystem, and why Swagger pulls toward classes
When class-validator is the wrong choice
When Standard Schema is the wrong choice
pages.text: NestJS 12 ships two validation stacks, and neither is deprecated. The classic one runs class-validator 0.15.1 over a decorated DTO class; the new one runs any Standard Schema — Zod, Valibot, ArkType — attached to the parameter. This page is the argument about which to use, and it ends with an actual recommendation rather than "it depends". If you have not read the two mechanically, start with The ValidationPipe and Standard Schema with Zod. This page assumes you know what each looks like. The same contract, twice Both reject the same requests. The differences are everywhere except the happy path. The comparison Dimension class-validator + ValidationPipe Standard Schema + StandardSchemaValidationPipe Shape A class whose properties carry decorators A value you import Type-inference direction Class first — the TypeScript type is the source, constraints are annotations on it Schema first — the runtime schema is the source, the type is derived with z.infer Can type and check disagree? Yes. age: string with @IsInt() compiles and fails at runtime No. The type is the schema's output Build requirements experimentalDecorators, emitDecoratorMetadata, reflect-metadata Nest's own decorators only; no metadata emit Dependencies Two pre-1.0 peers you version yourself One schema library Unknown keys Pipe-level: whitelist, forbidNonWhitelisted Schema-level: z.strictObject(), .onUndeclaredKey('reject') Enforcement default Global pipe covers every class-typed parameter automatically Opt-in per parameter; a missing schema is silently unvalidated Conditional and cross-field rules Custom validator with registerDecorator, or @ValidateIf .refine() / .superRefine() on the schema Injecting a provider into a rule Supported — a @ValidatorConstraint class plus useContainer() Not supported by the pipe; do the lookup in the service Reuse outside HTTP The class validates microservice and queue payloads too The schema validates anything, including config at boot OpenAPI First-party: @nestjs/swagger 12.0.1 reads the decorators Convert the schema yourself — z.toJSONSchema() or a zod-to-OpenAPI package Transformation class-transformer via @Type(), @Transform(), transformOptions Built into the schema: .transform(), .default(), z.coerce Refactoring safety Renaming a property leaves its decorators attached; deleting a decorator is silent Renaming a key changes the inferred type, so call sites fail

pages.title: Whitelisting and unknown properties
pages.description: How whitelist and forbidNonWhitelisted stop mass assignment in NestJS 12, the Zod strictObject equivalent, and a worked exploit that escalates a user to admin through an unfiltered body.
headings: Do not rely on the pipe alone
Nested objects need the same treatment
pages.text: An HTTP body is a bag of keys an attacker chose. Validation tells you the keys you expected are acceptable; it says nothing about the ones you did not expect. Deciding what happens to those is the single most consequential validation setting in a Nest application, and both validation stacks get it wrong by default. This page is the control in detail: whitelist and forbidNonWhitelisted on ValidationPipe, z.strictObject() on the schema side, and a worked exploit that turns an ignored field into an admin account. Why it exists class-validator only knows about properties that carry a decorator. Everything else is invisible to it — and by default, invisible means untouched, not removed. The pipe validates email, finds no problem, and hands your service an object that still has every other key the client sent. That object then reaches something that iterates its keys: an ORM's create() or save(), an Object.assign(), a { ...body } spread into an entity. The database column the attacker guessed gets written. This is mass assignment, and the Nest-specific detail is that a validated payload can still carry it. The exploit A profile-update endpoint. The DTO is careful, the pipe is registered, and every field the client is allowed to send is constrained. A validated body is not a filtered body The pipe was configured with the default options: The User entity has a role column, because the application has roles. The DTO does not mention it — which is exactly why nothing checks it. Two hundred, not four hundred. displayName passed @MaxLength(80), role was never looked at, and Object.assign wrote it. The attacker did not bypass validation — validation ran and approved the request. The same hole exists with a Prisma update({ data: body }), a Mongoose findByIdAndUpdate(id, body), a Drizzle .set(body), and any hand-written { ...entity, ...body }. The ORM is not the bug; handing it unfiltered input is. The fix Two options on the pipe, and they are a pair. Option Effect whitelist: true Strips every property that has no validation decorator from the value the handler receives. forbidNonWhitelisted: true Changes stripping into rejection. Requires whitelist: true — on its own it does nothing at all. whitelist: true alone is safe: role never reaches the service. forbidNonWhitelisted: true on top of it is better, because the client finds out. pages.title: Transforming payloads
pages.description: What transform, enableImplicitConversion, @Type() and @Transform() really do in NestJS 12, how query and param strings become numbers, and how the Standard Schema pipe's transform differs.
headings: Primitive conversion for path and query parameters
Converting fields inside a DTO with @Type()
Transformation in the Standard Schema stack
pages.text: Validation answers "is this acceptable". Transformation answers "what does my handler actually receive". The two run in the same pipe, in that order, and most of the confusion about ValidationPipe comes from assuming one option controls both. NestJS 12 has two transformation stories, matching the two validation stacks: class-transformer 0.5.1 driven by transform and transformOptions, and the schema's own output under StandardSchemaValidationPipe. What transform: true actually does With transform: false — the default — the pipe validates a temporary instance and then hands your handler the original plain object. Every @Type() conversion, every getter, every @Transform() is discarded. With transform: true, the pipe returns the instance it built: Concretely, transform: true gives you three things: A real instance. body instanceof CreateUserDto is true, so methods and getters on the DTO work. Applied conversions. @Type(() => Number) and @Transform() survive into the handler. Primitive conversion on named path and query parameters — a narrower feature than it sounds, covered below. It does not strip unknown keys. That is whitelist. The two are independent options that people routinely conflate, and transform: true, whitelist: false is a validated object with every extra key still attached. The `transform: false` path is subtler than "returns the input" When validation succeeds and transform is off, the pipe returns the original value — unless you passed more than one validator option, in which case it returns a classToPlain() of the validated instance instead. That is an implementation detail you should never have to reason about, and the way to never reason about it is to set transform: true and move on. Primitive conversion for path and query parameters Everything in a URL is a string. @Param('id') id: number is '42' at runtime, not 42, and typeof id === 'string' no matter what the annotation says. transform: true fixes this, but only under three conditions, all of which come from the pipe's own transformPrimitive step: the parameter names a property — @Param('id') or @Query('page'), not bare @Param() or @Query(); the parameter type is param or query — never body; the reflected metatype is Number, Boolean or String. The conversion rules are exactly as narrow as they look. Number is +value, so a non-numeric string becomes NaN and is handed to your handler — tran

pages.title: Serialization
pages.description: Controlling what a NestJS 12 response actually contains — ClassSerializerInterceptor with @Exclude and @Expose, the new StandardSchemaSerializerInterceptor, and why a response schema is what stops a password hash leaking.
headings: The trap: it only works on instances
@Exclude() is a denylist. Prefer an allowlist.
Three behaviors to know before you rely on it
pages.text: Validation decides what enters your application. Serialization decides what leaves it, and it is the half people skip. A handler that returns the entity it just loaded returns every column on that entity — including the password hash, the password-reset token, the internal risk score and the soft-delete flag — because nothing between return user and the JSON body removes them. NestJS 12 gives you two interceptors for this, matching the two validation stacks: ClassSerializerInterceptor with class-transformer decorators, and the new StandardSchemaSerializerInterceptor with a Standard Schema. The leak Every column you did not think about is in the response The password hash is offline-crackable. The reset token is an account takeover: request a reset for the victim, read this endpoint, use the token. Neither requires a bug anywhere else in the application. Adding a column is a migration. Adding a column to a public API response should be a decision. Without a serialization layer, the first is silently the second. The fix, with class-transformer Mark what must never leave, and turn the interceptor on. Prefer the provider form so the interceptor exists in tests built from AppModule: ClassSerializerInterceptor loads class-transformer lazily at construction, so the same 0.5.1 peer dependency the validation stack uses is required here. The trap: it only works on instances The interceptor calls classToPlain() on whatever the handler returned. classToPlain reads @Exclude() metadata from the value's class. Hand it a plain object and there is no class, no metadata, and no exclusion — it returns everything, with no error. This is not a rare edge case. It is the normal result of: Prisma, which returns plain objects from findUnique(); Mongoose with .lean(); Drizzle and raw drivers, which return row objects; any service that builds { ...user, fullName } before returning; TypeORM's getRawOne() / getRawMany(). TypeORM's repository methods do return entity instances, which is why the example above works and why a later refactor to a query builder silently reopens the hole. Two ways to close it. Construct the instance yourself: Or tell the interceptor which class to use, with the type option: When type is set and the value is not already an instance of it, the interceptor runs plainToInstance() first and then classToPlain(). That is the supported way to serialize a plain object

pages.title: Connections and DI
pages.description: A database connection is a provider in the Nest container — forRootAsync with ConfigService, custom providers wrapping a pg Pool, module scoping, and closing the pool on shutdown.
headings: The three ways to get a connection into the container
A custom provider wrapping a pg Pool
The service that owns the lifecycle
Why the connection must be a singleton provider
Module scoping — who can inject what
pages.text: Everything on the rest of these pages follows from one idea: in Nest, a database connection is a provider. It is constructed once by the injector, handed to whoever declares it as a dependency, and destroyed when the application shuts down. That is a different lifecycle from the module-level export const pool = new Pool() you would write in a plain Express app, and the difference is what makes configuration, testing and shutdown work. How the examples are written Nest's constructor injection is usually written with the TypeScript parameter-property shorthand, constructor(private readonly repo: Repository<User>) {}. The snippets here declare the field and assign it in the constructor instead, because the site's snippet checker type-strips every ts block and parameter properties are emitting syntax. The two forms are exactly equivalent — use the shorthand in your own code. Why it exists A plain Node app resolves its database handle through the module graph: import { pool } from './db.js'. That works, and Part 1 documents it that way. It also has three properties that hurt once the app is more than one file: Configuration is read at import time. The Pool is constructed the moment the module is first imported, which is before ConfigModule has validated anything and before a test has had a chance to point it somewhere else. There is no seam. Nothing can substitute the pool. Every test that touches a repository touches the real database at the real URL. Nobody owns shutdown. pool.end() has to be called from a SIGTERM handler that imports the pool from the other side of the app. Making the connection a provider fixes all three at once. The factory runs when the injector builds the module — after config, in an order Nest controls. overrideProvider gives tests a seam. And a provider implementing OnModuleDestroy is closed by the framework. The three ways to get a connection into the container Approach Use it for What you get An integration module — TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync, MongooseModule.forRootAsync ORMs with a Nest package The connection, plus repository/model providers, plus health indicators A custom provider — { provide: TOKEN, useFactory, inject } Raw drivers (pg, mysql2, ioredis), Prisma, Drizzle Total control; you write the lifecycle hook A @Injectable() service that owns the client Prisma, and anywhere you want methods alongside the handle A class token, s

pages.description: Wiring the pg driver into a Nest application — a pooled provider built from ConfigService, parameterised repository methods, SQLSTATE to HttpException mapping, and closing the pool on shutdown.
headings: The service that owns the pool
pages.text: The pg driver does not change inside Nest. What changes is who owns it: instead of a module-level export const pool, the pool is a provider the injector builds after configuration has been validated and destroys when the application closes. This page is about that wiring. The driver mechanics — Pool versus Client, type parsers, ON CONFLICT, SSL, rowMode — are in PostgreSQL with pg and are not repeated here. What Nest actually changes Plain Node Inside Nest new Pool() at import time a useFactory that runs after ConfigModule validated the environment process.env.DATABASEURL read inline config.getOrThrow('DATABASEURL'), so a missing value fails the boot pool.end() in a SIGTERM handler onModuleDestroy() on the provider, driven by app.enableShutdownHooks() nothing can substitute the pool overrideProvider(PGPOOL) in a testing module every module imports db.js only modules that import DatabaseModule can reach the database Everything else — $1 placeholders, statementtimeout, SQLSTATE codes — is identical. Installing pg is a pure-JavaScript driver, so there is no native build step and nothing to rebuild in your Docker image. Node 24 LTS is the target; pg 8 has no unusual engine requirement. The pool provider Connections and DI builds this provider in full. The short version, so this page stands on its own: Two of those options are worth the keystrokes on every project: statementtimeout is set on the connection, so every query on it is bounded whether or not the calling code remembered. Without it one missing index during an incident holds a pool slot for minutes. See Retries and timeouts. applicationname shows up in pgstatactivity. When four services share a database, it is the difference between "something is holding locks" and "the export worker is holding locks". idleintransactionsessiontimeout is the safety net for a transaction that was opened and never finished — an await that threw between BEGIN and COMMIT in code that forgot its finally. Typed configuration ConfigService.get('DBPOOLMAX') returns whatever was in the environment, which is a string. Reading it straight into max gives you a pool of "10", and pg will not complain. Use registerAs so the coercion happens once: @nestjs/config 12 accepts any Standard Schema for validationSchema, so the Zod schema from Configuration works directly. A missing DATABASEURL is then a refusal to start, not a 500 on the firs

pages.title: MySQL
pages.description: The mysql2 promise pool as a Nest provider — ConfigService-driven options, execute with ? placeholders, mapping MySQL error codes to HttpExceptions, and ending the pool on shutdown.
headings: The service and the shutdown hook
pages.text: mysql2 gives you a pool with its own end(), its own error codes and a prepared-statement cache. Inside Nest all three become lifecycle concerns the container can manage for you. The driver detail — execute versus query, type coercion flags, charset, LASTINSERTID() — is in MySQL with mysql2; this page covers only the wiring. Installing Always import from mysql2/promise. The root export is the callback API, and mixing the two in one codebase produces methods that return undefined where you expected a promise. The pool provider The options that change behaviour rather than performance: Option Why it is set this way waitForConnections: true A borrow request queues instead of throwing instantly when the pool is full. queueLimit: 0 Unbounded queue. Bound it (e.g. 100) if you would rather shed load than queue — then a full pool is a fast 503. enableKeepAlive: true Managed MySQL and most load balancers drop idle TCP connections silently; without keepalive the first query after a quiet period fails. namedPlaceholders: true Enables :name placeholders alongside ?. Both are still parameters. timezone: 'Z' Without it the driver converts DATETIME using the server process's local zone, so the same row reads differently on a laptop and in a container. decimalNumbers: false The default. DECIMAL arrives as a string, which is correct — turning it on silently loses precision on money columns. `multipleStatements` stays off multipleStatements: true lets one call run several statements separated by ;. It also turns every parameterised query into a potential injection point, because a value that escapes its quoting can then append a whole second statement rather than just distorting one. Leave it false (the default). If a migration tool needs it, give that tool its own connection — not the application pool. The service and the shutdown hook pool.end() is a promise in mysql2/promise; awaiting it inside onModuleDestroy is what makes Nest wait for it. It only runs at all if main.ts calls app.enableShutdownHooks(). execute, not query execute prepares the statement on the server and sends the values separately, so a value can never become syntax. query interpolates client-side using the driver's escaping — safer than string concatenation, but it is still one escaping bug away from injection and it gives up the statement cache. Use execute everywhere; reach for query only for the handfu

pages.title: SQLite
pages.description: better-sqlite3 and node:sqlite as Nest providers — synchronous access inside an async framework, PRAGMAs applied in onModuleInit, prepared-statement caching, and where SQLite is and is not a production answer.
headings: Where SQLite fits in a Nest service
pages.text: SQLite is the odd one out in this section: there is no pool, no network, and the API is synchronous. That makes the Nest wiring simpler than any other driver and introduces exactly one new concern — a synchronous query blocks the event loop for every other request in the process. The engine itself, WAL mode, the single-writer model and the PRAGMA set are covered in SQLite; this page is about living with it inside a Nest application. Which library node:sqlite better-sqlite3 13.0.3 Install built in from Node 22.5, stable enough to teach on 24 native module, needs a compiler or a prebuilt binary API synchronous synchronous Statement cache you keep the StatementSync you keep the Statement Extensions, backup API, user functions limited extensive Docker image nothing to add a build stage or a matching prebuild Prefer node:sqlite when it covers what you need — a zero-dependency database in a Nest service is a genuinely good deal, and it removes a native build from your image. Reach for better-sqlite3 when you need its backup API, custom SQL functions, or WAL checkpointing control. Both are used identically from a Nest provider, so switching later is a one-file change. The provider There is no pool, so the provider is the database handle itself. It is still a singleton, still built from validated config, and still closed by a lifecycle hook. fileMustExist deserves the conditional. In development you want the file created on first run; in production a typo in the path should be a boot failure, not a silently empty database serving 404s. PRAGMAs belong in onModuleInit SQLite's defaults are tuned for an embedded device, not a server. Three of them have to be changed on every connection, and onModuleInit is the place — it runs after the handle exists and before any controller is reachable. foreignkeys = ON is the one people lose data to. It is off by default and it is a per-connection setting, so a foreign key declared in your schema does nothing until you turn it on — deletes cascade into nothing and orphan rows accumulate for months before anybody notices. node:sqlite instead The same provider with the built-in module: DatabaseSync exposes exec(), prepare() and close(), so SqliteService above needs only its pragma() calls rewritten as this.db.exec('PRAGMA journalmode = WAL'). Prepared statements as provider state prepare() compiles a statement. Doing it on every reque

pages.title: MongoDB
pages.description: MongooseModule.forRootAsync and forFeature in Nest 12, decorator schemas, ParseObjectIdPipe, and the operator-injection hole that a global ValidationPipe closes.
headings: 2. Type the filter value at the query site
pages.text: @nestjs/mongoose turns a Mongoose connection into a provider and each model into an injectable token. That part is mechanical. The part that matters is that MongoDB takes a query object, and an object parsed from JSON can contain operators — so a request body that reaches a filter unchecked is an authentication bypass, not a validation nicety. This page covers the wiring and that hole. The driver-level material — projections, indexes, aggregation, the replica-set requirement for transactions — is in MongoDB. Installing @nestjs/mongoose 12 targets Nest 12 and Mongoose 9. It manages the connection lifecycle, so you do not call mongoose.connect() yourself and you do not close it on shutdown — the module's own provider does, given app.enableShutdownHooks(). The connection MongooseModuleOptions extends Mongoose's own ConnectOptions, plus a handful of Nest-specific keys: Key What it does uri The connection string. MongooseModule.forRoot(uri, options) takes it as the first argument instead. retryAttempts / retryDelay How many times Nest retries the initial connection before failing the bootstrap. Nothing to do with reconnects later. connectionName Names a second connection so its tokens do not collide with the default. onConnectionCreate Runs once with the Connection, which is where event listeners belong. lazyConnection Skips connecting during bootstrap. Useful in tests; means the first query pays the connect cost. connectionFactory Wraps the connection — the hook global plugins are registered from. verboseRetryLog Logs the reason for each retry rather than just the attempt number. serverSelectionTimeoutMS is the one to set deliberately. It defaults high, and a wrong hostname then presents as a 30-second hang on the first request rather than a fast failure at boot. Schemas and models forFeature registers a provider whose token is getModelToken(User.name); @InjectModel(User.name) is shorthand for @Inject(getModelToken(User.name)). Like TypeORM's forFeature, it is scoped to the module that imported it — another module that wants the User model must import forFeature itself, or (better) go through UsersService. @nestjs/mongoose 12 also ships ParseObjectIdPipe and IsObjectIdPipe, so a route parameter becomes a real ObjectId before the service sees it: Without it, findById('not-an-id') throws a CastError that surfaces as a 500. pages.title: Redis
pages.description: Redis in a Nest application two ways — @nestjs/cache-manager 12 with cache-manager 7 and @keyv/redis for cache-aside, and a raw ioredis provider for everything the cache abstraction cannot express.
headings: The CacheInterceptor, and when not to use it
pages.text: Redis shows up in a Nest application in two distinct roles, and conflating them causes most of the trouble. As a cache it belongs behind @nestjs/cache-manager, which gives you a store-agnostic interface and lets tests run against memory. As a data structure server — locks, rate-limit counters, streams, pub/sub, sorted sets — it needs the real client, and that means a custom provider. This page wires up both. The command-level material is in Redis. Two stacks, one process @nestjs/cache-manager 12.0.0 a raw ioredis 6.0.0 provider Interface get / set / del / wrap / mget every Redis command Underlying client @keyv/redis 5.1.6, which uses @redis/client ioredis Swap to memory in tests one line no Locks, INCR, streams, pub/sub, Lua no yes TTL unit milliseconds seconds (EX) or milliseconds (PX) Running both in one process is normal and correct — they are different jobs. It does mean two connections; size for that. The cache stack cache-manager 7 is built on Keyv: a "store" is a Keyv instance, and @keyv/redis is the Redis adapter. @nestjs/cache-manager 12 declares cache-manager >= 6 and keyv >= 5 as peer dependencies, so both are installed explicitly. Four details that are easy to get wrong: TTLs are milliseconds. ttl: 60 is sixty milliseconds, which looks exactly like a cache that does not work. This changed in cache-manager 6; examples written for 5 use seconds. stores is an array and it is tiered: a [new Keyv(), createKeyv(url)] pair gives you an in-process L1 in front of Redis. Useful, but be certain you can tolerate a stale L1 on the replicas that did not see the invalidation. namespace prefixes every key. Set it per service, so two applications sharing a Redis cannot collide and SCAN-based cleanup is scoped. isGlobal: true is justified here for the same reason it is for config: the cache is a cross-cutting concern, and threading an import through every feature module buys nothing. Using it Inject either the Cache class token or CACHEMANAGER. They resolve to the same instance; the class token avoids an @Inject(). wrap is the whole cache-aside pattern, including single-flighting: several concurrent requests for a cold key run the loader once rather than all stampeding the database. Writing that by hand with get / set and getting the race right is more code than it looks. The cache interface from cache-manager 7 is small and worth knowing in full: get, mget, set,

pages.title: Connection pooling
pages.description: Sizing a pool inside a Nest application — one singleton pool per process, what replicas multiply, the serverless pool-explosion problem, and exposing pool counters as metrics and a health signal.
headings: One pool per process, enforced by the container
Borrow latency is the leading indicator
Leaks, and the Nest-shaped way to cause one
pages.text: The arithmetic of connection pooling is the same in Nest as anywhere else, and Connection pooling does that arithmetic: why a pool of 100 is usually slower than a pool of 10, how exhaustion presents, and what a transaction-mode pooler breaks. What Nest adds is a place to put the pool — one singleton provider — and a container that makes it easy to accidentally create more than one. One pool per process, enforced by the container A provider is a singleton by default: one instance for the whole application, built once. That is the correct cardinality for a pool, and it is the reason the DI approach beats a module-level global — not because it is tidier, but because the container is the only thing that knows how many exist. Three ways to end up with more pools than you think: A second unnamed forRoot. TypeOrmModule.forRoot() registered in two modules does not add a second connection — it replaces the first, and queries start going to the wrong database. A genuine second connection needs name. A @Module that lists the pool provider instead of importing its module. Nest resolves providers per module unless the module that owns them exports them and you import that module. Re-declaring { provide: PGPOOL, useFactory } in a feature module runs the factory again. You now have two pools of ten, both open, and only one is closed if only one service implements onModuleDestroy. Import DatabaseModule instead. A request-scoped provider in the chain. Marking anything request-scoped propagates upward through everything that injects it. If a pool provider becomes request-scoped, you build a pool per request: At 200 requests per second that is 200 pools per second, each opening TCP connections and TLS handshakes, none of them closed. maxconnections is gone in seconds. Read Injection scopes before making anything request-scoped. The rule from Connections and DI holds throughout this section: the connection is a singleton; the unit of work is a parameter. Where the size is set Each integration has its own name for the same number. pages.title: Transactions
pages.description: Making a transaction span several Nest services — passing the EntityManager or Prisma tx client explicitly versus AsyncLocalStorage, why REQUEST scope is the wrong tool, and never wrapping an outbound HTTP call.
headings: Option 1 — pass the unit of work explicitly
Why REQUEST scope is the wrong tool
QueryRunner, when the callback is not enough
Never hold a transaction across an outbound call
Side effects belong after the commit
pages.text: Transactions in Nest are hard for one structural reason: the container hands every service a repository bound to the pool, and a transaction lives on a single connection. Two services injected side by side get two different connections, so a "transaction" that calls across them commits half its work and rolls back the other half — with no error. Everything on this page is about closing that gap. The database-level material — isolation levels, lost updates, FOR UPDATE, deadlock retries — is in Transactions and still applies unchanged. The problem, concretely The transaction() callback opens a transaction on one checked-out connection and never gives it to anyone. StockService.reserve runs on a different connection and auto-commits. OrdersService.create runs on a third. Throw from orders.create and the stock reservation stays. Worse, the reservation can deadlock against the empty transaction the callback is holding. Nothing about this fails loudly. It passes review, it passes a test that only asserts the happy path, and it produces a support ticket six weeks later about inventory that does not match orders. There are exactly two mechanisms that fix it. Pick one for the whole codebase. Option 1 — pass the unit of work explicitly Every method that participates takes the transaction as a parameter. Repositories never reach for the injected handle when one is supplied. The default parameter — tx: EntityManager = this.em — is what makes this tolerable. A service method still works when called outside a transaction, so you are not forced to thread a manager through read paths that do not need one. What is good about this: the transaction boundary is visible in every signature. A reviewer can see, without running anything, whether a call participates. A method that forgot the parameter is a type error the moment the caller passes one. What is bad: it is viral. Adding a transaction to an operation touches every method beneath it, and a repository with fifteen methods grows fifteen optional parameters. On a large codebase that friction is real and people route around it. Best practice Take the friction as a signal. If passing tx through six layers feels absurd, the operation probably should not span six layers. Two services that must commit together are frequently one unit of work that got split for the wrong reason. Prisma is the same shape with a different type. The

pages.title: Migrations
pages.description: Migrations as a deploy-pipeline step for a Nest service — never on boot with multiple replicas, a TypeORM DataSource the CLI can read, prisma migrate deploy, expand/contract, and a DDL user separate from the app user.
headings: The two settings that cause data loss
TypeORM: a DataSource the CLI can read
Expand and contract, on a Nest timeline
pages.text: A migration is a schema change, and a Nest application is usually several replicas starting at once. Those two facts settle the central question of this page: migrations run once, in the deploy pipeline, before the new replicas start — never from onModuleInit, never from migrationsRun: true, never from synchronize: true. Forward-only migrations, expand/contract, index locking and the cost of each DDL operation are covered in Migrations; this page is about running them around a Nest deployment. The two settings that cause data loss synchronize: true derives DDL from whatever entity files the running process loaded and applies it on start. A renamed property is a dropped column, and the data in it is gone with no migration file and no record. A deploy of the wrong branch rewrites production's schema. It is not a "development convenience with a production caveat" — it is a loaded weapon pointed at whatever database the process happens to connect to, including the one your integration tests point at. Fail the bootstrap if it is ever true outside development: migrationsRun: true runs pending migrations from DataSource.initialize(). With one replica that is merely bad practice. With three replicas rolling out simultaneously it is three processes racing the same ALTER TABLE: TypeORM takes an advisory lock around its migration run on Postgres, so two replicas usually serialise rather than corrupt. "Usually" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and MySQL has no equivalent. The replica that waits blocks its own startup behind the migration, so a slow migration fails its readiness probe and the orchestrator restarts it — mid-migration. The migration runs as the application database user, which means that user must own the schema. That is the permission you most want it not to have. A failed migration is now a failed pod, and the orchestrator's response is to try again. A partially-applied DDL retried in a loop is a genuinely bad afternoon. The deploy pipeline The shape that works, in order: Build the image. It contains the compiled application and the compiled migrations. Run migrations as a separate one-shot step — a Kubernetes Job, an ECS task, a release command — using the same image and the DDL credentials. Wait for it to succeed. A non-zero exit stops the deploy before any new replica starts. Roll out the new replicas with the application credentials. backoffL

pages.description: Seeding a Nest application through NestFactory.createApplicationContext so seeds reuse your providers — idempotent upserts, reference data versus demo data, and never putting test accounts in production.
headings: Two kinds of seed, kept apart
Never seed production with test accounts
Where seeding sits in the deploy
pages.text: A seed script written outside the application ends up with its own database connection, its own password-hashing code and its own idea of what a valid user looks like — and all three drift. Nest has a better answer: NestFactory.createApplicationContext boots the module graph with no HTTP server, so a seed can inject the same services the API uses. The database-level material — idempotency, deterministic fake data, truncate-and-reload — is in Seeding; this page is about doing it through the container. Two kinds of seed, kept apart They have different lifecycles, different audiences and different risks. Conflating them is how demo accounts reach production. Reference data Development / demo data Examples countries, currencies, plan tiers, permission names, feature flags 500 fake users, sample orders, a signed-in demo account Where it runs every environment, including production local and ephemeral preview environments only How it runs as part of the deploy, after migrations by hand, or when a preview environment is created Must be idempotent yes it is recreated from scratch anyway Lives in src/database/seeds/reference/ src/database/seeds/dev/ Keep them in separate directories with separate entry points. A single seed script with an if (isDev) branch is one merge away from running the wrong half. A standalone application context createApplicationContext gives you the container without a listener: providers are constructed, onModuleInit runs, and app.get() resolves anything the module graph exports. Four things that make this worth doing over a standalone script: The seeder is a provider. It injects UsersService, PasswordHasher, ConfigService — the real ones. A seeded password is hashed by the same code that verifies it at login, which is not true of a script that reaches for argon2 directly. Configuration is validated. The same ConfigModule schema runs, so a seed cannot silently connect to the wrong database because DATABASEURL was unset. app.close() closes everything. Pools, Redis clients, scheduled timers. A script that forgets this leaves the process hanging, and the usual "fix" is a process.exit(0) that also abandons in-flight writes. process.exitCode = 1 on failure. A seed that logs an error and exits 0 is a deploy step that cannot fail, which means it is not a deploy step at all. What `createApplicationContext` also does It constructs every provider in Ap

pages.title: Health checks
pages.description: Database health checks with @nestjs/terminus 12 — HealthCheckService, the TypeORM, Mongoose, memory and disk indicators, a custom indicator with HealthIndicatorService, and why liveness must never touch the database.
pages.text: @nestjs/terminus gives you a health controller that composes indicators and renders a consistent JSON result. What it does not give you is judgement about which checks belong in which probe — and getting that wrong is how a 60-second database failover becomes a 20-minute outage. Health checks explains that failure mode in detail and is worth reading first; this page is the Nest implementation. Installing @nestjs/terminus 12 declares engines.node: ^20.19.0 || ^22.12.0 || >=24.0.0 and peers on @nestjs/common and @nestjs/core 11 or 12. Its database indicators are optional peer dependencies: TypeOrmHealthIndicator needs typeorm and @nestjs/typeorm installed, MongooseHealthIndicator needs mongoose and @nestjs/mongoose, PrismaHealthIndicator needs @prisma/client. You install only the ones you use. The two probes They answer different questions and the difference is not stylistic — it is determined by what the orchestrator does when each fails. Liveness Readiness Question Is this process broken beyond repair? Should it receive traffic right now? On failure restart the container remove from the load balancer Touches the database no yes Touches Redis no only to report degraded Path /livez /readyz The rule follows mechanically: a liveness probe may only fail for conditions a restart would fix. A restart does not fix an unreachable database, a saturated pool, or a provider outage — so none of those belong in liveness. The most expensive Terminus mistake During a database failover every replica's liveness probe fails at once, Kubernetes restarts every pod simultaneously, and the database — already recovering — is hit by a reconnect storm from every cold replica. The new pods fail their probes too. CrashLoopBackOff. The database recovers in 60 seconds. Your service does not recover for 20 minutes, because it destroyed itself. Had liveness ignored the database and readiness checked it, the outcome would have been: pods stay up, traffic drains, the database recovers, readiness passes, traffic returns. Total impact: 60 seconds, with warm pools. The health module TerminusModule.forRoot() takes optional options; imports: [TerminusModule] on its own is equivalent to the defaults. It exports HealthCheckService, HealthIndicatorService and every built-in indicator, so the controller just injects what it needs. pages.title: Retries and timeouts
pages.description: Bounding database work in a Nest service — statement timeouts on the connection, AbortSignal.timeout(), a retry provider with backoff and jitter, which errors are retryable, and a circuit breaker that fails fast.
headings: The interceptor timeout does not cancel the query
pages.text: Every database call needs an upper bound on how long it may take and a decision about what happens when it fails. Nest adds two wrinkles to that: the framework's own TimeoutInterceptor ends the request without stopping the query, and TypeOrmModule's retryAttempts covers only the initial connection — both of which read like they solve the problem and do not. The general material on backoff, jitter, idempotency keys and circuit breaking is in Retries and timeouts. Timeouts at every layer A request that reaches a database passes through several bounds. Each one must be shorter than the one outside it, or the outer bound fires first and the inner work keeps running. Layer Where it is set in Nest Typical Client / load balancer outside the app 30 s HTTP server keep-alive and headers server.requestTimeout, headersTimeout 20 s Request-level interceptor RxJS timeout() in an interceptor 10 s Connection acquisition connectionTimeoutMillis / connectTimeout 5 s Statement execution statementtimeout on the pool 5 s Transaction lifetime idleintransactionsessiontimeout, Prisma timeout 10 s The one that does real work is statementtimeout, because it is enforced by the server: the database stops executing and returns an error. Everything above it merely stops waiting. Set it on the connection, not per call site. A connection-level bound is the only one that covers the code path nobody remembered to wrap, and it is the difference between one slow query and a pool full of them. Where a specific query legitimately needs longer, raise it for that transaction only: SET LOCAL, never SET. A session-scoped SET statementtimeout = '60s' on a pooled connection is inherited by whichever request borrows it next, and you have quietly removed the bound from a random slice of your traffic. MySQL has no connection-wide equivalent for writes. maxexecutiontime covers SELECT only, and per-statement it is an optimizer hint: For everything else on MySQL the bounds are innodblockwaittimeout, waittimeout, and your own AbortSignal — which is why the MySQL page treats this as a real gap rather than a footnote. The interceptor timeout does not cancel the query This is the Nest-specific trap. This is worth having — it stops a request hanging forever. But understand exactly what it does: it unsubscribes from the observable and sends a 408. The promise underneath keeps running. The query is still executing

pages.title: Testing with a database
pages.description: Testing Nest services against a real database — overriding the datasource in Test.createTestingModule, throwaway SQLite versus disposable Postgres, per-test isolation by transaction rollback, and migrations in the test bootstrap.
headings: Mock the boundary, not the database
pages.text: A mocked repository proves that your service calls the methods you told it to call. It cannot prove that the query is valid SQL, that the column exists, that the unique constraint fires, that the transaction rolls back, or that the migration you wrote last week matches the entity. Those are the bugs that reach production, and the only thing that catches them is a real database. Nest makes this cheap: Test.createTestingModule is the same container with a seam for substituting the connection. Mock the boundary, not the database There is a real place for mocks — the payment provider, the email service, the clock. The database is not one of them. Test Mocked repository Real database Service calls findOne passes passes The SQL is valid not tested fails at the query The column exists not tested fails at the query A unique constraint rejects the duplicate not tested 23505 A transaction rolls back on throw not tested row is absent The migration matches the entity not tested fails at bootstrap ON DELETE CASCADE behaves not tested tested An N+1 happened not tested visible in a query count The mock's whole output is a restatement of the test's own setup. See Mocking providers for where mocks do earn their place. Throwaway SQLite or disposable Postgres Both are legitimate; they buy different things. SQLite (:memory: or a temp file) Postgres in a container Start-up milliseconds seconds Parallel test files trivial — one database each one schema or one database each CI dependencies none a service container or Docker Dialect fidelity different engine identical to production Catches invalid SQL, missing columns, constraint logic, rollback all of that, plus everything below What SQLite cannot catch, when production is Postgres: Types. SQLite has no real BOOLEAN, DATE, NUMERIC, UUID, JSONB, or array type. A DECIMAL column is a float, true is 1, and a timestamp is a string. Rounding and comparison bugs hide here. Postgres-only SQL. ON CONFLICT, RETURNING, window functions, CTEs, ILIKE, generateseries, ANY($1::bigint[]), LATERAL. A repository that uses any of them cannot run under SQLite at all. Concurrency. One writer, no FOR UPDATE, no deadlocks, no isolation levels. Every test on this page about locking is untestable. Constraint timing. Deferred constraints, partial and expression indexes, exclusion constraints. Case and collation. Identifier folding and ORDER BY collation di

pages.title: Choosing an ORM
pages.description: TypeORM, Prisma, Mongoose, Drizzle and raw drivers inside NestJS 12 — what a first-party module actually buys you, how each one behaves in a DI container, and when no ORM is the right answer.
headings: What a first-party module actually buys you
What each one is genuinely good at inside Nest
pages.text: Nest does not pick a data layer for you. It picks the shape of the integration: whatever you use has to become a provider, has to be constructed after configuration is validated, and has to be closed on shutdown. That shape is the same for all five options on this page — what differs is how much of it somebody has already written. The library-level comparison (types, migrations, weight, escape-hatch safety) is in Comparison table and is still correct; this page is only about the decision inside Nest. Why it exists Two of these tools ship a Nest package and three do not, and that fact dominates the first week of a project in a way the library comparison does not capture. A first-party module is not just convenience — it decides who owns the connection lifecycle, what a unit test has to mock, and whether a health check is one line or thirty. The second Nest-specific factor is the repository seam. Nest's whole value is that dependencies arrive through a constructor, so the question "can I replace this with a fake in Test.createTestingModule()?" has a different answer for each tool. Get that wrong and every test needs a database. The five options Option Nest package Version What you write yourself TypeORM @nestjs/typeorm 12.0.1 with typeorm 1.1.1 Entities and migrations Mongoose @nestjs/mongoose 12.0.0 with mongoose 9.9.5 Schemas Prisma none @prisma/client 7.10.0 A PrismaService and a PrismaModule — about 25 lines Drizzle none drizzle-orm 0.45.2 A custom provider, a token, and the shutdown hook Raw drivers none pg 8.23.0, mysql2 3.24.4, better-sqlite3 13.0.3 The pool provider, the repository layer, the SQL Warning TypeORM is on the 1.x line. Any Nest tutorial that calls createConnection(), getRepository() as a global or @EntityRepository predates it. And the npm latest tag for prisma is 8.0.0-rc.13, a release candidate — pin prisma@7 and @prisma/client@7. What a first-party module actually buys you Four concrete things, and it is worth knowing them individually because you can reproduce all four by hand in an afternoon. 1. Lifecycle ownership. TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync and MongooseModule.forRootAsync connect during bootstrap and disconnect on shutdown. With Prisma or Drizzle, you write the OnModuleInit/OnModuleDestroy hooks — and if you forget, the failure is a rolling deploy that severs open connections rather than an error anyone sees. See Connections and DI.

pages.title: TypeORM
pages.description: TypeORM 1.1.1 inside NestJS 12 with @nestjs/typeorm 12.0.1 — forRootAsync, forFeature, injected repositories, transactions, migrations and keeping the query builder parameterised.
headings: Injecting the DataSource and the EntityManager
Do not return entities from controllers
Named parameters in the query builder
pages.text: @nestjs/typeorm is the first-party module that turns a TypeORM DataSource into a Nest provider and every entity repository into an injectable token. Almost everything else — entities, relations, the query builder, migrations — is plain TypeORM, documented in depth on TypeORM. This page covers the Nest half: wiring, injection, transaction boundaries in a DI container, and the escape hatches you have to keep parameterised. This page documents @nestjs/typeorm 12.0.1 with typeorm 1.1.1. Warning TypeORM is on the 1.x line. createConnection(), getConnection(), getManager(), getRepository() as a global, @EntityRepository and string arrays for relations were all removed in 1.0. If a Nest tutorial calls any of those, it predates the current library — see TypeORM for the full removal list and the codemod. Why it exists Without the module you would construct a DataSource, call initialize() somewhere in main.ts, and import a repository singleton into every service. That works, and it makes those services untestable without a database, because the repository is a module-level import rather than a constructor dependency. @nestjs/typeorm gives you three things instead. forRoot/forRootAsync register the DataSource as a provider and let Nest own its lifecycle — connect on bootstrap, destroy() on shutdown. forFeature registers one provider per entity so a repository arrives through the constructor. And because they are ordinary providers, Test.createTestingModule().overrideProvider(getRepositoryToken(User)) replaces them in a unit test with no database at all. When to use it Class-based entities with relations as object properties, especially if the team is coming from Hibernate, Doctrine or Entity Framework. A database the TypeScript-first ORMs skip — Oracle, SAP HANA, Spanner, MSSQL. You want a first-party Nest module. TypeORM and Mongoose are the only two ORMs with one; everything else is a custom provider you maintain. When not to use it You want exact query types. find({ select: { id: true } }) still returns the entity type. Prisma and Drizzle narrow it. You cannot enable decorators. Entities need experimentalDecorators and emitDecoratorMetadata. In a Nest project you already have both, so this rarely bites — but it does rule out running the app with Node's type stripping. Cold-start-sensitive deployments. Entity metadata is built at initialize() and startup cost scales

pages.title: Prisma
pages.description: Prisma 7.10.0 inside NestJS 12 — the PrismaService provider, a PrismaModule, driver adapters, relation queries, both $transaction forms, the raw escape hatch, and why you must pin prisma@7.
headings: Client extensions and the class pattern
Do not return Prisma results from controllers
Map Prisma errors to HTTP in one filter
Prisma.sql, Prisma.join and Prisma.empty compose safely
The application user is not the migration user
pages.text: There is no @nestjs/prisma. The integration is a provider you write: a class that extends PrismaClient, implements OnModuleInit and OnModuleDestroy, and is exported by a small module. That is about twenty-five lines, and it is the officially documented approach — not a workaround. Everything about the library itself (the schema DSL, prisma.config.ts, migrations, client extensions) is in Prisma; this page covers the Nest half. This page documents @prisma/client 7.10.0 with prisma 7 and @prisma/adapter-pg 7.10.0. Pin `prisma@7` The npm latest dist-tag for prisma points at 8.0.0-rc.13, a release candidate, while @prisma/client latest is the stable 7.10.0. An unpinned npm install prisma in a fresh CI container gives you an RC CLI against a v7 client — a mismatched pair, and an RC in your pipeline. Why it exists PrismaClient owns a connection pool and has to be a singleton. In a plain Node app you export one from a module and import it everywhere. In Nest that is the pattern Connections and DI argues against: it is constructed at import time, before ConfigModule has validated anything, nothing can substitute it in a test, and nobody closes it on SIGTERM. Wrapping the client in a provider fixes all three. The instance is built by the injector after configuration is available, overrideProvider(PrismaService) gives tests a seam, and onModuleDestroy closes the pool when the framework tears the app down. There is a second, subtler reason to use a class rather than a useFactory. A class is its own injection token, so services declare constructor(prisma: PrismaService) with no @Inject() decorator — which keeps Prisma out of the decorator noise in every file that touches the database. When to use it A new TypeScript service on PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite, SQL Server or CockroachDB. This is Prisma's home ground and the default recommendation in Choosing an ORM. You want migrations you did not write. prisma migrate dev diffs the schema against a shadow database and emits SQL. Mixed-seniority team. The client is hard to misuse and the errors are readable. When not to use it MongoDB. Prisma 7 dropped support. Use Mongoose. SQL is your primary interface. Window functions, recursive CTEs and GROUP BY ROLLUP all mean dropping to $queryRaw, which is a hard boundary — you leave the type system and hand-annotate the row type. Drizzle fits better. You cannot add a build step.

pages.title: Mongoose
pages.description: Mongoose 9.9.5 with @nestjs/mongoose 12.0.0 — forRootAsync and forFeature, @InjectModel, decorator schemas with SchemaFactory, select:false, populate without N+1, transactions on a replica set, and sanitizeFilter.

Hooks and plugins in a Nest codebase
Fix two: cast explicitly at the query site
sanitizeFilter, and when to reach for mongoose.trusted()
The raw escape hatch bypasses everything
pages.text: @nestjs/mongoose is one of the two first-party ORM modules. It registers the Mongoose Connection as a provider, turns each schema into an injectable model token, and lets you declare schemas with decorators instead of a new Schema({...}) literal — so a schema file reads like the rest of a Nest codebase. The library itself is covered in Mongoose, and the connection options and operator-injection threat in depth in MongoDB. This page is the ORM-shaped half: schemas, models, relations and the patterns that go wrong. This page documents @nestjs/mongoose 12.0.0 with mongoose 9.9.5. Warning Mongoose 9 removed callback support across the API and changed middleware signatures: a pre hook no longer receives next — hooks are async functions or return promises. Most Mongoose material online predates this. If a snippet calls next() in a pre hook or passes a callback to save(), it is Mongoose 7 or earlier. Why it exists MongoDB accepts any document you send it. Two years in, the users collection holds four different shapes and every read path needs defensive checks. Mongoose enforces shape at the application boundary instead — schema, casting, validators, hooks. What @nestjs/mongoose adds on top is the container. The Connection becomes a provider with a lifecycle Nest owns, forFeature registers one provider per model so a service receives a narrow dependency, and getModelToken(User.name) is the seam a unit test overrides. Without it you would import { User } from '../models/user.js' at module scope, and every test that touches a service would touch a real database. When to use it The database is MongoDB. This is effectively the decision — Prisma 7 dropped MongoDB entirely, so the real question is Mongoose or the raw driver. You want validation and defaults close to the data. Required fields, enums, custom validators, declared once on the schema class. Cross-document references. populate() is the practical answer to MongoDB having no join in the query language you usually want to write. Lifecycle hooks. Hashing before save, stamping audit fields, cascading a soft delete. When not to use it Aggregation-heavy analytics. You will live in aggregate(), where the schema layer mostly gets in the way. Use the driver — MongoDB. Bulk ingest. Casting and validating a million documents costs real time. bulkWrite, or the driver. Your data is a graph of joins with transactional integri

pages.title: Drizzle
pages.description: Drizzle ORM 0.45.2 inside NestJS 12 — there is no @nestjs/drizzle, so the integration is a custom provider with a DRIZZLE token, a useFactory, your own shutdown hook, and the sql versus sql.raw rule.
headings: A health indicator, since there is not one
Keep the schema import out of your controllers
Do not put the pool in a controller
pages.text: Drizzle is a thin, fully typed SQL builder: you define tables in TypeScript and the query you write maps almost one-to-one onto the statement that gets sent. There is no runtime engine, no code generation and no hidden rewriting. The library itself is covered in Drizzle; this page is the Nest integration. This page documents drizzle-orm 0.45.2 with drizzle-kit 0.31.10 and pg 8.23.0. There is no first-party `@nestjs/drizzle` Nest ships integration modules for TypeORM and Mongoose only. Everything below is a community pattern built from ordinary Nest primitives — a custom provider, a token and a lifecycle hook. It is not a package you install and it is not blessed by either project. If you find a third-party wrapper, weigh it against the thirty lines below: a wrapper you do not control sits between you and two libraries that both move, and this one is small enough to own. Consequences you own rather than inherit: the connection lifecycle, bootstrap retries, the health indicator, and the token naming if you connect to more than one database. Note A 1.0.0-rc.4 exists on the rc dist-tag, and the official documentation site has largely moved to that v1 API — most visibly, v1 replaces relations() with defineRelations(). The latest tag is still 0.45.2, which is what this page covers. A relations snippet copied from the website that uses defineRelations will not compile here. Why it exists You reach for Drizzle in Nest for two reasons the other options do not give you together. The SQL stays visible. db.select().from(posts).where(eq(posts.authorId, id)) is one readable step from SELECT … FROM posts WHERE authorid = $1. When a query is slow you read it, not the ORM's interpretation of it. And CTEs, window functions, ON CONFLICT and FOR UPDATE are first-class rather than a drop to a raw string. It weighs almost nothing. Zero runtime dependencies, no engine binary, no metadata build at startup. Bootstrap costs whatever constructing a pg pool costs — which matters if you deploy to anything that cold-starts, and which is the opposite end of the range from TypeORM building entity metadata at initialize(). The price is the missing module, and it is smaller than it looks: the whole integration is one useFactory. When to use it Your team knows SQL and wants to keep knowing it. Cold start or bundle size is a real constraint — serverless, edge, workers. You need SQL features ro

pages.title: Raw drivers
pages.description: When an ORM is the wrong tool inside Nest — reporting queries, bulk operations and exact plan control — and how to wire a pg Pool as a provider with parameterised queries, typed rows and a clean shutdown.
headings: When an ORM is the wrong tool
A service that is small enough
When not to drop to the driver
Multi-row insert with a parameterised VALUES list
pages.text: An ORM is a trade: it buys you type safety, migrations and relation loading, and it charges you a query language that is narrower than SQL. For most of an application that is a good trade. For reporting, for bulk work, and for anything where you need to control the plan, it is not — and the answer is not to fight the ORM, it is to drop to the driver for those paths and keep the ORM for the rest. This page is about doing that inside Nest without giving up the container. Verified versions: pg 8.23.0, mysql2 3.24.4, better-sqlite3 13.0.3. The pg provider in full — typed config, SQLSTATE mapping, schema-per-tenant — is in PostgreSQL; this page is about when to reach for it and how it coexists with an ORM. How the examples are written Nest's constructor injection is usually written with the parameter-property shorthand, constructor(private readonly db: PgService) {}. The snippets here declare the field and assign it, because the site's snippet checker type-strips every ts block. The two forms are equivalent — use the shorthand in your own code. When an ORM is the wrong tool Reporting queries Window functions, recursive CTEs, GROUP BY ROLLUP, LATERAL joins, DISTINCT ON, FILTER (WHERE …) aggregates. Every query API in this section either cannot express these or expresses them through a raw escape hatch — at which point you have the raw string plus the ORM's ceremony around it. The honest version of "we use Prisma" is "we use Prisma for the CRUD surface and a pg pool for eleven reporting queries", and that is a better codebase than one where those eleven queries are $queryRaw calls pretending to be part of the model layer. Bulk operations Per-row ORM calls cost a round trip and an object allocation each. A single statement does not. pages.title: Repository vs active record
pages.description: TypeORM 1.1.1 supports both patterns — why static entity methods fight a DI container, how a repository provider gives you a test seam and a transaction boundary, and how to keep ORM types out of your services.
headings: What you actually lose with active record in Nest
Mongoose sits in between, and the module fixes it
Keeping ORM types out of your services
Level 2 — a repository provider per aggregate
Level 3 — a port and an adapter
Never return an entity from a controller
pages.text: Active record puts persistence on the entity: user.save(), User.findOne(...). The repository pattern — TypeORM calls it data mapper — puts it on a separate object: usersRepository.save(user). TypeORM supports both, Mongoose documents are active-record-shaped, and Prisma, Drizzle and raw drivers only do the second. Inside Nest the choice is not a matter of taste, because one of the two has no injection token. Why it exists A Nest application is a graph of providers. Everything the framework gives you — constructor injection, overrideProvider in tests, module boundaries, request-scoped context, interceptors that wrap a provider — operates on instances the container built. A static method on a class is none of those things. It is reachable from anywhere, it is bound to whatever DataSource somebody assigned it at bootstrap, and nothing can substitute it. That is the entire argument, and everything below is a consequence of it. How the examples are written Nest's constructor injection is usually written with the parameter-property shorthand, constructor(private readonly users: Repository<User>) {}. The snippets here declare the field and assign it, because the site's snippet checker type-strips every ts block. The two forms are equivalent — use the shorthand in your own code. The two styles in TypeORM Active record The entity extends BaseEntity and gains statics (find, findOne, create, update, delete) and instance methods (save, remove, softRemove, recover, reload). It reads beautifully, and in a Rails-shaped application it is a perfectly good pattern. In Nest it has a wiring problem before it has a design problem: those statics need a DataSource, and @nestjs/typeorm hands you the DataSource as a provider, not as a global. You have to bind it yourself, at bootstrap, before anything queries: That provider is the whole problem in miniature: a lifecycle hook whose job is to install a global, so that code which does not participate in the container can work anyway. Repository (data mapper) The entity is data. A Repository<User> arrives through the constructor. Same query, same SQL. The difference is that UsersService now declares what it needs, and the container decides what to give it. When an N+1 is actually fine
pages.text: An N+1 is one query to fetch a list, then one more query per item in that list. It is invisible on a laptop, it is the largest single win available in most slow endpoints, and Nest adds two places to hide it that plain Express does not have: an interceptor and a serializer both run after your service returned, so a query issued there is one nobody reading the service will see. The framework-independent version of this page — the latency arithmetic, the = ANY($1) patterns, a DataLoader implementation in forty lines — is N+1 queries, and all of it still applies. How the examples are written Nest's constructor injection is usually written with the parameter-property shorthand. The snippets here declare the field and assign it, because the site's snippet checker type-strips every ts block. The two forms are equivalent — use the shorthand in your own code. A concrete N+1 An endpoint returning the 50 most recent posts with each post's author: The queries are not slow. Each is an indexed primary-key lookup the database answers in about 0.2 ms. The cost is the round trip, and it is entirely invisible where you develop: Deployment Round trip 51 queries, serially 2 queries Database in Docker on your laptop 0.15 ms 8 ms 0.5 ms Same availability zone 0.8 ms 41 ms 2 ms Cross-AZ, TLS 2.5 ms 128 ms 5 ms At 100 requests per second that endpoint issues 5,100 queries per second against a database that needed to answer 200. It also occupies a pooled connection for the whole sequence, so the failure it eventually produces looks like pool exhaustion rather than a code problem. Connection pooling. await inside a for loop over query results is the shape to look for. `Promise.all` is not the fix await Promise.all(posts.map((p) => this.users.findOne(…))) runs the fifty queries concurrently, so wall-clock time improves. It is still fifty queries, it now wants fifty pooled connections at once — which you do not have — and forty-eight of them queue anyway. You have converted a latency problem into a pool-exhaustion problem. Reduce the number of queries; do not parallelise them. Where it hides in a Nest application The loop above is the easy case, because it is visible. These are not. An interceptor or a serializer.
